Introduction Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) is now the most common presentation of acute coronary syndrome, accounting for most cases of myocardial infarction in large registries [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]. Defined electrocardiographically by the absence of persistent ST-segment elevation, NSTEMI is not a single disease entity but a final common phenotype shared by patients with markedly different underlying mechanisms. While several specific subtypes have been identified, challenges remain in nomenclature, diagnosis, and treatment. In this review, we summarize the pathophysiology, classification, epidemiology, and angiographic phenotypes of NSTEMI and discuss mechanism-specific treatment.

2. Literature Search This narrative review is based on a search of the English-language literature indexed in PubMed/MEDLINE from database inception through 2026, supplemented by manual review of the reference lists from key articles and current society guideline documents. Search terms included combinations of “NSTEMI”, “non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome”, “Type 1 myocardial infarction”, “Type 2 myocardial infarction”, “myocardial injury”, “universal definition”, “MINOCA”, “spontaneous coronary artery dissection”, “revascularization”, “dual antiplatelet therapy”, and “intravascular imaging”. Priority was given to randomized controlled trials, large registries, contemporary society guidelines, and authoritative review articles and scientific statements. Given the narrative format, the selection of cited literature reflects the judgment of relevance by the authors rather than adherence to a formal systematic review protocol.

3. NSTEMI: Pathophysiology and Treatment 3.1 Historical Perspective For much of the 20th century, the immediate cause of acute myocardial infarction (AMI) was debated in the literature. A thrombus was identified at autopsy in most, but not all, cases, raising the question of whether it was the primary cause or secondary to reduced coronary blood flow from another mechanism. This debate was effectively settled in 1973 at a National Institutes of Health workshop attended by leading pathologists, clinicians, cardiologists, and hematologists. The consensus conclusion was that the weight of evidence supported a primary role for intracoronary thrombus as the immediate cause of transmural myocardial infarction (MI) at autopsy, a finding that closely correlates with the current definition of ST-elevation MI (STEMI) [ 4 ].

However, pathologic analyses at autopsy demonstrated that not every patient dying from AMI had either transmural necrosis or intracoronary thrombus. In many such cases, necrosis was partial and predominantly involved the inner layers of the myocardium. These were classified as non-transmural or subendocardial infarctions [ 5 ]. In the 1970s and 1980s, clinical and electrocardiogram (ECG) criteria were developed for non-transmural MI and included chest pain typical of myocardial ischemia lasting >15 minutes, new persistent ST depression or T-wave inversions, and elevated cardiac enzyme levels without new Q waves [ 6 ]. This definition was criticized as misleading because it did not consistently correlate with pathologic findings. Patients classified as having non-transmural infarction by ECG could have transmural infarction at autopsy. In the 1990s, in part to shift from a pathologic to a clinical classification, acute MI was redefined as ST-elevation versus non-ST-elevation MI (STEMI vs. NSTEMI), and the earlier terms were largely discarded. This designation persists today, and various types of NSTEMI have been recognized based on differing mechanisms. These mechanisms are discussed in the next section.

The 2007 American College of Cardiology (ACC)/American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines for the management of patients with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome (ACS) provide excellent definitions of NSTEMI pathophysiology, summarized as follows [ 7 ]. (1) The most common underlying molecular and cellular pathophysiology of disrupted atherosclerotic plaque (the predominant mechanism of STEMI and NSTEMI) is arterial inﬂammation, typically triggered by noninfectious stimuli ( e . g ., oxidized lipids), which can lead to plaque expansion and destabilization, rupture or plaque erosion, and thrombogenesis. Activated macrophages and T lymphocytes at the shoulder of the plaque increase the expression of enzymes, such as metalloproteinases, that cause thinning and disruption of the plaque, potentially leading to plaque rupture and subsequent unstable angina (UA)/NSTEMI (as well as STEMI). (2) A less common mechanism is dynamic coronary obstruction, triggered by intense focal spasm of a segment of an epicardial coronary artery (Prinzmetal’s angina). This local spasm results from hypercontractility of vascular smooth muscle and/or endothelial dysfunction. Large-vessel spasm may occur on top of obstructive or destabilized plaque. Dynamic coronary obstruction can also arise from diffuse microvascular dysfunction; for example, due to endothelial dysfunction or abnormal constriction of small intramural resistance vessels. Coronary spasm is also the presumed mechanism underlying cocaine-induced UA/NSTEMI. (3) Another mechanism is severe fixed coronary narrowing with or without superimposed spasm or thrombus. This occurs in some patients with progressive atherosclerosis or with restenosis after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). (4) Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is an important cause of NSTEMI, particularly in women. (5) A further common cause of NSTEMI is myocardial necrosis due to a supply–demand mismatch extrinsic to the coronary vascular bed. Patients may or may not have underlying coronary artery disease, and the NSTEMI is precipitated by conditions such as acute anemia, hypotension, severe hypoxia, tachycardia, heart failure, or severe hypertension. (6) Additional categories not included in the 2007 summary include myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA) [ 8 ]. This category may overlap with several of the mechanisms above but will be discussed separately later in this review. Furthermore, the pathophysiology of MI has been expanded to include plaque erosion and calcified nodules. A defect in the endothelium with overlying thrombus (plaque erosion) has been increasingly recognized on intravascular imaging, particularly optical coherence tomography (OCT), in NSTEMI [ 9 ]. Small OCT studies in selected patients with NSTEMI suggest that plaque erosion may be a common cause of NSTEMI, occurring in approximately 40% of cases, which is higher than the proportion observed in STEMI [ 9 ]. Calcified nodules as a cause of MI (either STEMI or NSTEMI) are more often seen in older patients or those with renal failure, in whom intracoronary thrombus formation develops on nodular calcium protruding into the vessel lumen [ 10 ].

3.2 NSTEMI Epidemiology According to a 2025 review in The Cardiology Advisor (February 13, 2025), there are roughly 780,000 cases of ACS annually in the United States (US), and approximately 70% (≈546,000) are NSTEMI. Males outnumber females by about 3:2, consistent with broader ACS epidemiology [ 1 ]. These estimates are based on population-level data using contemporary definitions of MI and encompass all etiologic subtypes classified under the Universal Definition (see below). Data from National Cardiovascular Data Registry (NCDR) programs provide two complementary “real-world” views. First, in the CathPCI Registry (patients undergoing PCI), 667,424 PCI procedures were performed in 2014 across 1612 US hospitals. Among indications, NSTEMI was more common than STEMI (≈17.9% vs. 15.8% of all PCIs or about 118,000 NSTEMI PCIs), approximating the annual volume of Type 1 NSTEMI cases that proceed to revascularization in this registry [ 2 ]. Second, in the later Chest Pain–MI Registry (all MI presentations at participating centers) between January 2019 and June 2020, 325,783 MI cases were recorded, including 91,262 STEMIs—implying that the majority (234,521) were NSTEMIs [ 3 ]. While these numbers do not capture all NSTEMI cases in the US (because of non-participating hospitals), these data underscore that NSTEMI is substantially more frequent than STEMI. Moreover, these data do not include the vast majority of Type 2 NSTEMIs (see below).

Risk factors for coronary artery disease are highly prevalent in NSTEMI cohorts and include hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, obesity, and family history. For example, registry data show diabetes in 36–41% of NSTEMI patients, atrial fibrillation in ~9–12%, and a declining prevalence of active smoking over the last decade [ 11 ]. The mean or median age at presentation depends on the overall risk profile but generally falls in the mid-60s to early-70s, with a US median age of approximately 68 years for ACS overall [ 11 ].

3.3 Universal Definitions of Myocardial Infarction With the advent of increasingly sensitive troponin assays, the specificity of elevated troponin for myocardial infarction declined. Clinicians were frequently consulted about hospitalized patients with troponin levels above the upper reference limit but without signs or symptoms of cardiac ischemia. The key questions became: What is the correct diagnosis, and are all such patients considered to have an MI?

In 2007, the First Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (UDMI) was published to clarify the diagnosis of MI in the context of elevated troponin levels [ 12 ]. The UDMI divided myocardial infarction into five categories (see Table 1 ). A diagnosis of MI required a rise and/or fall of troponin values with at least one value above the 99th-percentile upper reference limit, together with clinical evidence of myocardial ischemia based on one or more of the following: ischemic symptoms, new ischemic ECG changes, development of pathological Q waves, or imaging evidence of new loss of viable myocardium or new regional wall-motion abnormality. In the absence of such clinical evidence, an elevated troponin level should be attributed to myocardial injury rather than infarction. The Fourth UDMI, published in 2018, did not substantially change this overarching framework [ 13 ].

This article mainly focuses on the two most important categories for clinical practice, Type 1 and Type 2 MI, which represent the most common presentations of MI in hospitalized patients. NSTEMI occurring after PCI or coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) is not addressed in this article.

Type 1 MI . Type 1 MI corresponds to the first category described in the prior 2007 ACC/AHA guidelines. According to the UDMI, Type 1 is caused by atherothrombosis of an epicardial artery due to plaque rupture, plaque erosion, or a calcified nodule [ 12 ]. Thrombotic total occlusion of an epicardial coronary artery from these pathophysiological mechanisms is most common in STEMI, whereas total occlusion is less common in Type 1 NSTEMI.

Intravascular imaging, particularly with OCT performed during invasive coronary angiography immediately before percutaneous coronary intervention, has been crucial for understanding the in vivo pathophysiology of Type 1 MI. With an axial resolution of approximately 10–15 μm, OCT can reliably distinguish most cases of plaque rupture from plaque erosion or calcified nodules. Type 1 NSTEMIs share the same fundamental mechanisms as STEMIs, but as noted above, the culprit artery is less likely to be totally occluded. When total occlusion is present, it may involve a smaller myocardial territory ( e . g ., a branch vessel), a vessel with established collateral circulation, or a vessel with intermittent total occlusion. In other cases, multivessel coronary disease may be present, and a single culprit lesion or artery may be difficult or impossible to identify.

Type 2 MI . According to the UDMI, Type 2 MI refers to an MI (either STEMI or NSTEMI) in which myocardial ischemia/necrosis with troponin elevation is primarily caused by factors extrinsic to the coronary vascular bed, such as acute severe anemia, hypotension, severe hypoxia, leading to a significant supply–demand mismatch. The UDMI also includes epicardial causes that are not due to acute coronary atherothrombosis, including spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD), coronary spasm, and coronary embolization, as potential mechanisms for Type 2 MI. Differentiation between Type 1 and Type 2 MI is necessary because management strategies differ between these entities. However, in many cases, the distinction between Types 1 and 2 is not apparent, leading to diagnostic uncertainty and challenges in therapeutic decision-making.

Problems With Type 2 Diagnosis An elevation in troponin above the upper reference limit may reflect either myocardial injury or myocardial infarction. When this biomarker is applied to the diagnosis of Type 2 MI, there is marked non-uniformity. Across the literature, the reported incidence of Type 2 MI among patients with acute MI ranges from <5% to >70% [ 14 ]. Thus, it is unlikely that such a wide range can be explained solely by baseline differences in the studied population. We believe several problems inherent to the current Type 2 MI definition contribute to this variability. Furthermore, a recent systematic review has highlighted that Type 2 MI remains underrepresented or inadequately distinguished from Type 1 MI in major NSTEMI clinical trials, underscoring the need for more precise enrollment criteria and dedicated therapeutic studies for this population [ 15 ].

Based on expert opinion, we previously summarized the difficulties with a Type 2 diagnosis in an article published in the American Journal of Cardiology [ 16 ]. These include the following: (1) According to the UDMI, neither the degree of supply–demand mismatch nor the type of symptoms is standardized for Type 2 MI diagnosis. (2) Troponin values that fluctuate just above and below the upper reference limit can be interpreted as a flat pattern rather than a clear rise and fall. All of these issues promote subjective interpretation and, in turn, diagnostic non-uniformity. (3) Symptoms may vary considerably, further confusing clinicians. Studies reporting a very high incidence of Type 2 MI may classify heart failure patients who present with a small troponin increase and dyspnea as the only clinical evidence of myocardial ischemia as having myocardial infarction, rather than diagnosing these patients with myocardial injury [ 17 ]. While dyspnea can be an anginal equivalent, the near-universal presence of this condition in heart failure exacerbations renders this complaint highly nonspecific. Thus, Type 2 MI can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed. In one study, patients with unequivocal Type 2 MI, as determined by experienced cardiologists on retrospective chart review, were compared with hospital discharge diagnoses in a blinded fashion; fewer than 10% were correctly diagnosed during the index hospitalization [ 17 ]. (4) Additional issues with the UDMI definition of Type 2 MI relate to the inclusion of epicardial conditions such as SCAD, epicardial spasm, and coronary embolization. Prior studies have identified factors extrinsic to the coronary vascular bed as causes of acute coronary syndromes. In 1939, a pathological study described patients with myocardial necrosis in the absence of intracoronary thrombus, suggesting that the necrosis might have been caused by factors extrinsic to the coronary vascular bed [ 5 ]. Similarly, in 1989, Braunwald [ 18 ], in his classic paper on unstable angina, classified some cases as secondary to extrinsic forces that reduce the coronary supply–demand ratio.

In that same publication [ 16 ], the following changes to the UDMI definition of Type 2 MI were proposed to reduce diagnostic variability: (1) To align with the pathological data and the Braunwald unstable angina definition, epicardial causes of Type 2 MI should be included as a subcategory of Type 1 MI. Thus, Type 2 MI should be reserved for processes extrinsic to the coronary vascular bed. (2) In patients presenting with a congestive heart failure (CHF) exacerbation and a small troponin increase, dyspnea as the only clinical evidence of myocardial ischemia should not automatically be considered indicative of Type 2 MI but rather of myocardial injury. (3) In our estimation, the most fundamental problem with the Type 2 MI diagnosis is how to interpret a small increase in troponin above the upper reference limit and what constitutes a significant supply–demand mismatch. Both parameters are subjective and prone to personal interpretation. We hope that a fifth UDMI will address these issues to improve the standardization of Type 2 MI diagnosis.

3.4 Angiographic Findings in Type 2 NSTEMI The diagnosis of Type 2 MI should be based on specific clinical criteria rather than coronary anatomy alone. Angiographic data in Type 2 MI indicate that significant coronary artery disease may be present in approximately 50–60% of cases, particularly in older patients with multiple comorbidities [ 14 ]. However, acute thrombotic culprit lesions caused by plaque rupture/erosion are not present [ 13 ]. In the remaining cases, in which coronary anatomy is evaluated, the findings may include non-obstructive disease or no identifiable plaque on invasive angiography. However, these estimates are imprecise, as most patients with Type 2 MI do not undergo coronary evaluation. This variable coronary anatomy likely contributes to the vagueness of current diagnostic criteria for Type 2 MI.

3.5 Angiographic Findings in Type 1 NSTEMI In 1985, a prior report first described the angiographic characteristics of culprit lesions in unstable angina [ 19 ]. This work predated intravascular imaging, and little information was then known regarding the pathophysiology of unstable angina. We described that, in more than two-thirds of patients, the culprit lesion had severe obstruction and was eccentric on orthogonal views, with irregular borders, overhanging edges, or filling defects. These lesions were initially termed “type 2 eccentric” and later classified as complex lesions. Compared with culprit lesions in patients with stable angina, this complex lesion morphology was 71% sensitive and 84% specific for unstable angina. Based on a study by Levin and Fallon [ 20 ], irregular stenoses on post-mortem angiography in patients who died from MI had “complicated” histology characterized by plaque disruption and/or thrombus. Thus, it was postulated that these complex lesions identified in vivo on invasive angiography in unstable angina represented plaque disruption and/or intracoronary thrombus formation (Fig. 1 , Ref. [ 19 ]).

Fig. 1. Coronary angiogram from a patient who presented with a Type 1 NSTEMI . The arrow highlights an eccentric culprit lesion with overhanging plaque edges in the distal left circumflex coronary artery (LCX). First described by Ambrose et al. (1985) [ 19 ], these lesions were classified as Type II eccentric lesions and were thought to represent plaque disruption, a partially occlusive thrombus, or both.

Clinically, unstable angina presented similarly to NSTEMI, but without elevation of cardiac enzymes consistent with AMI. With the introduction of troponin, a more sensitive marker than creatine kinase–myocardial band (CK-MB) for detecting myocardial necrosis in the 1980s, many patients previously described as having unstable angina would now be diagnosed with NSTEMI. As troponin assays became increasingly sensitive, the proportion of patients labeled with unstable angina declined further, prompting Braunwald and Morrow to publish a “requiem” for unstable angina in Circulation in 2013, noting its marginalization as ultrasensitive troponin assays converted most unstable angina presentations to NSTEMI [ 21 ].

What, then, are the angiographic findings in Type 1 NSTEMI? The answer depends on several factors, including age, sex, the number of risk factors, and the type of NSTEMI. A previous study assessed the angiographic findings in 193 patients with either Type 1 STEMI (n = 73) or NSTEMI (n = 120) [ 22 ]. In Type 1 NSTEMI, an identifiable culprit lesion was found in 56% of patients, and the majority (73%) of these lesions were complex, as described above. Non-obstructive/normal coronary arteries or 3-vessel disease were observed in 10% and 27% of patients, respectively. A culprit lesion could still be identified in 43% of those with 3-vessel disease.

At least one additional study attempted to identify the culprit lesion in patients with NSTEMI and multivessel disease using cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). In a prospective three-center study, 114 patients with first-presentation NSTEMI underwent delayed-enhancement cardiac MRI (DE-CMR) followed by coronary angiography [ 23 ]. With the interventionalist blinded to CMR findings, the infarct-related artery (IRA) was identifiable by angiography in 63% of cases. DE-CMR identified an IRA in 60% and also established a new non-CAD diagnosis in 19% of patients.
In our opinion, there are at least two NSTEMI presentations that are not classical but relatively common and must always be considered in any comprehensive discussion of NSTEMI.

3.5.1 MINOCA MINOCA accounts for roughly 5–10% of MI presentations and is an umbrella term encompassing several pathophysiologies, including atherosclerotic plaque disruption/erosion, epicardial or microvascular spasm, SCAD, and thromboembolism, after excluding non-ischemic mimics such as Takotsubo syndrome [ 24 ]. Invasive angiography and echocardiography are often inconclusive for establishing the underlying mechanism [ 8 ]. The PROMISE trial, a small investigation, evaluated a structured diagnostic strategy for patients with MINOCA. This approach included cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) for tissue characterization, OCT when plaque instability was suspected, acetylcholine testing for vasomotor disorders, and echocardiography to search for embolic sources, followed by etiology-tailored therapy vs. standard care [ 24 ]. In this study, stratified management improved Seattle Angina Questionnaire summary scores by about 9 points at 12 months (a clinically important change) and identified a mechanism in 80% of patients. Epicardial spasm was most frequent (~36%), followed by plaque instability (~22%), SCAD (~13%), and embolism/microvascular spasm (each ~4%). The initial bedside impression could be reclassified in approximately 75% of cases. Although the study was underpowered for hard outcomes, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs) were numerically lower with stratified care, without added procedural harm, supporting the concept that mechanism-guided therapy is important in MINOCA. In practice, MINOCA should be considered only after non-ischemic causes ( e . g ., Takotsubo syndrome) have been excluded. However, we believe that MINOCA is sometimes overdiagnosed in clinical practice. Anecdotally, at our institution, several cases labeled as MINOCA were in fact compatible with Type 2 MI (unpublished observations). Whenever feasible, in the absence of an obvious Type 2 MI or another clear etiology, we believe additional testing—if available—should be pursued and may include CMR and/or intravascular or functional testing [ 24 ].

3.5.2 SCAD SCAD is a major non-atherosclerotic cause of ACS (often presenting as NSTEMI), especially in younger women and in those with peripartum status, fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD), or emotional/physical stress precipitants (Table 2 ) [ 25 ]. The underlying pathology is an intramural hematoma and/or an intimal tear compressing the true lumen. Clinically, SCAD more often presents as NSTEMI than STEMI. Large registries report roughly two-thirds NSTEMI and one-third STEMI ( e . g ., SCAD: ~70% NSTEMI and ~30% STEMI), with similar distributions in multicenter cohorts ( e . g ., 56% NSTEMI and 42% STEMI in a 389-patient series) [ 26 ]. Pregnancy-associated SCAD tends to present more frequently as STEMI [ 26 ].

In patients whose initial presentation mimics ACS but is ultimately attributed to SCAD, intravenous systemic anticoagulation is not routinely continued. While many patients receive unfractionated heparin (or other anticoagulants) early in the emergency department under standard ACS protocols, expert consensus recommends discontinuing anticoagulation once SCAD is suspected/confirmed [ 27 ]. Since SCAD is driven by an intramural hematoma and/or dissection plane, anticoagulation could theoretically promote hematoma expansion and propagation of the dissection. Therefore, anticoagulation should be reserved for clear alternative indications, such as atrial fibrillation with cardioembolic risk, left ventricular thrombus, venous thromboembolism, or mechanical valve, rather than used reflexively as part of routine ACS therapy in SCAD. In those rare situations, the risk–benefit balance may favor continued short-term anticoagulation with close monitoring. However, such decisions should be individualized and frequently reassessed in light of the competing risk of hematoma progression.

Coronary intervention in SCAD is technically challenging (because of the risk of wiring the false lumen and propagating the dissection). Invasive therapies are generally reserved for ongoing ischemia, left main involvement, or hemodynamic compromise. OCT or intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) should not be performed routinely in all suspected cases of SCAD; however, it should be considered when the diagnosis remains uncertain and the expected benefit outweighs the procedural risk. Many patients stabilize with conservative management alone, and spontaneous angiographic healing is common over weeks. Stenting is usually avoided unless there is ongoing ischemia and impaired blood flow distal to the SCAD that cannot be restored with balloon angioplasty alone. However, occasionally, stenting or even CABG may be required to salvage a large territory of myocardium, although overall mortality appears to be higher when CABG is performed.

Beta-blockers are used empirically to reduce shear stress; non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers may be helpful for vasospastic symptoms. Statins are not routinely used unless dyslipidemia is present [ 27 ]. Patients should be screened for associated arteriopathies ( e . g ., iliac/renal/carotid fibromuscular dysplasia) and counseled on trigger avoidance and pregnancy planning. Recurrent events and residual symptoms are not uncommon and warrant the need for close follow-up and referral to cardiac rehabilitation [ 27 , 28 ].

4. Treatment of NSTEMI: Type 1 vs. Type 2 Since patients frequently present before the underlying mechanism is clear, distinguishing Type 1 (atherothrombotic plaque rupture/erosion) from Type 2 (oxygen supply–demand mismatch) NSTEMI is essential but can be clinically challenging during the initial evaluation. Some patients may be managed initially along standard ACS pathways until additional data (clinical context and/or routine blood tests; ECG/echo findings; troponin kinetics; if performed, coronary imaging) clarify the etiology [ 29 ]. However, when an obvious supply–demand mismatch is present, such as active bleeding, severe tachycardia, or hypotension due to sepsis, then the event should initially be managed as a Type 2 MI.

In Type 1 NSTEMI, treatment generally follows evidence-based ACS care: intravenous anticoagulation, antiplatelet therapy, and high-intensity statin therapy with additional guideline-directed anti-ischemic therapies as appropriate. An in-hospital invasive strategy is usually appropriate with coronary angiography and revascularization (PCI vs. CABG) guided by coronary anatomy, ischemic risk, comorbidity burden, and Heart Team considerations [ 29 ]. These are all Class 1 recommendations in the current guideline [ 29 ].

In contrast, management of Type 2 NSTEMI primarily involves treating the precipitating condition ( e . g ., sepsis, hypoxemia, tachyarrhythmia, hypertensive crisis, profound anemia, or active bleeding), with individualized decisions regarding antithrombotic therapy given the absence of a primary atherothrombotic event [ 30 ]. Importantly, many patients labeled as having Type 2 MI/NSTEMI have underlying CAD. Thus, decisions about whether to pursue invasive or coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA), or only a noninvasive evaluation, should be individualized and consider several factors, such as the pre-test probability of obstructive CAD, symptom burden, hemodynamic stability, recurrent ischemia, ECG/imaging evidence of ischemia, bleeding risk, and overall clinical trajectory of each patient [ 30 ]. Based on the 2025 ACC/AHA ACS guidelines, when uncertainty exists, it is recommended to treat the event as Type 1 [ 29 ].

According to the guidelines, Class 1 recommendations for NSTE-ACS patients with Type 1 MI include parenteral anticoagulation for the index hospitalization. If unfractionated heparin is chosen, it should be continued for at least 48 hours or until PCI is performed with activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) monitoring. Fondaparinux reduces bleeding compared with enoxaparin in conservative strategies and is preferred when early PCI is not planned. If PCI is performed in a patient receiving fondaparinux, a single unfractionated heparin (UFH) bolus should be given to prevent catheter thrombosis. Enoxaparin is an acceptable alternative. Bivalirudin is reasonable in the cath lab, particularly if bleeding risk is high or if avoidance of GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors is desired [ 29 ].

4.1 DAPT in NSTEMI In NSTE-ACS after PCI, aspirin plus either ticagrelor or prasugrel is generally preferred over clopidogrel based on superior ischemic outcomes and more rapid, potent platelet inhibition. Clopidogrel remains reasonable for lower bleeding risk/tolerance issues, in patients administering direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), in the setting of drug–drug interactions, or cost/access limitations, and when CABG is likely [ 29 ].

Regarding early dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) before angiography, the 2023 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) ACS guideline is more restrictive, assigning a Class 3 (not recommended) indication against P2Y12 pretreatment when coronary anatomy is unknown and an early (<24 h) invasive strategy is planned. In contrast, the 2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline is more permissive in a narrow scenario, allowing a weak Class 2b option to consider upstream clopidogrel or ticagrelor when an invasive strategy is planned; however, angiography is expected to be delayed (>24 h) [ 29 , 31 ]. If an ischemia-guided strategy is not elected or invasive angiography is delayed, pretreatment may be reasonable in selected, low-bleeding-risk patients with either clopidogrel or ticagrelor [ 29 , 30 ].

In high bleeding risk (HBR) patients, who comprise up to 40–45% of those undergoing PCI, individualized balancing of ischemic and hemorrhagic risk is essential. HBR is defined by the Academic Research Consortium (ARC-HBR) criteria as the presence of at least one major or two minor risk factors ( e . g ., oral anticoagulant use, severe chronic kidney disease (CKD), recent bleeding, advanced age, thrombocytopenia), corresponding to a ≥4% annual risk of Bleeding Academic Research Consortium (BARC) 3 or 5 bleeding [ 32 ]. Fig. 2 (Ref. [ 33 ]) lists high-bleeding and high-thrombotic-risk features [ 33 ]. High thrombotic-risk features are associated with higher ischemic risk. Clinicians must balance ischemic and bleeding risk in patients with overlapping risk features. Registry data confirm that patients with both high bleeding and high thrombotic risk experience the highest absolute rates of both MACEs and major bleeding, and neither current guidelines nor existing trials provide a clear, evidence-based DAPT strategy for this overlapping population. Individualized decision-making, ideally with serial reassessment of evolving risk, remains the most prudent approach [ 34 ].

Both the 2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline and the 2023 ESC ACS guideline recommend 12 months of DAPT as the default strategy for patients not at high bleeding risk (Class 1). For HBR patients, the two guidelines diverge modestly. The 2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline provides a Class 1 recommendation for transitioning to ticagrelor monotherapy after ≥1 month of well-tolerated DAPT with ticagrelor post-PCI, supported by the TWILIGHT, TICO, and ULTIMATE-DAPT trials [ 29 ]. In contrast, the 2023 ESC guideline takes a more conservative approach, recommending P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy after 3–6 months of event-free DAPT in HBR patients who are not at high ischemic risk (Class 2a, A). Abbreviation of DAPT to 1 month is denoted only as a Class 2b recommendation. Notably, both guidelines advise against reducing DAPT within the first 30 days after ACS. A recent meta-analysis of randomized trials in HBR patients further supports a shortened DAPT duration (1–3 months) followed by P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy, with reduced bleeding without increased MACEs or stent thrombosis [ 35 ]. These considerations are particularly relevant when planning staged multivessel PCI, where cumulative contrast load, prolonged antiplatelet exposure, and procedural complexity compound bleeding risk. Another strategy of converting from ticagrelor to clopidogrel after one month (de-escalation) has also been studied [ 36 ]. In the 2025 ACC/AHA guidelines, de-escalation of DAPT after 1 month carries a weak Class 2b recommendation.

These criteria are summarized in Fig. 3 [ 29 ]. The timing of DAPT relative to angiography is discussed in the preceding section. For left main disease, randomized trials demonstrate broadly comparable mid-term outcomes between CABG and PCI. However, PCI is associated with higher rates of repeat revascularization and, in some analyses, higher late death/MI, especially in people with diabetes with high SYNTAX scores [ 38 , 39 , 40 ]. Both guidelines support the physiological assessment of non-culprit stenoses to guide revascularization (ACC/AHA Class 2b; ESC Class 2b) and mandate a multidisciplinary Heart Team approach that integrates coronary anatomy, left ventricular function, diabetes, frailty, stroke risk, and patient preference. In older or frail patients, viability testing, overall comorbidity burden, and goals of care often limit surgical plans. In such cases, culprit-only PCI, staged PCI, or hybrid strategies (culprit PCI initially, followed by CABG) remain reasonable options when clinical stability permits [ 39 , 40 ].

4.4 Complete vs. Culprit-Only Revascularization in NSTEMI With PCI For STEMI, several large randomized controlled trials (RCTs) (PRAMI, DANAMI-3-PRIMULTI, COMPLETE) support complete revascularization of suitable non-culprit lesions, usually in a staged fashion, thereby reducing reinfarction and repeat revascularization [ 40 , 41 , 42 ]. However, in Type 1 NSTEMI, there is no large, dedicated randomized clinical trial definitively establishing a complete-versus-culprit PCI strategy. While CABG typically achieves complete revascularization, evidence for complete revascularization with PCI is based on smaller trials and observational/meta-analytic data. The SMILE trial, a small, two-center study, suggested that complete revascularization (often staged) reduces the need for repeat ischemia/revascularization without clear safety penalties. In the SMILE trial (584 patients, two-center, unblinded), single-stage complete revascularization reduced the 1-year composite major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE) endpoint by approximately 45% compared with multistage PCI (13.6% vs. 23.2%), driven primarily by a 48% relative reduction in target vessel revascularization (8.3% vs. 15.2%). No significant differences were observed in the individual hard endpoints of death or reinfarction [ 43 ].

Additional data supporting complete revascularization were identified from FAMOUS-NSTEMI, a physiology-guided NSTEMI strategy, which showed that fractional flow reserve (FFR) can safely defer non-ischemic lesions and reduce stent use without worsening outcomes, implying that “functionally complete” rather than purely angiographically complete revascularization may be optimal [ 44 ]. Contemporary meta-analyses and registries generally favor treating significant non-culprit disease, either during the index procedure or staged, when lesion severity is supported by physiology or clear ischemia, with approximately 27–47% relative reductions in composite MACEs compared with culprit-only PCI [ 45 ]. Accordingly, the 2025 ACS guidelines provide a Class 1 recommendation in stable patients with NSTE-ACS and multivessel disease (MVD), without left main stenosis, who are not intended for CABG and who undergo culprit-lesion PCI: PCI of significant non-culprit lesions (at the time of the index procedure or as a staged procedure) is recommended to reduce the risk of MACEs [ 29 ].

Who benefits most from complete PCI? Younger patients with few comorbidities, clear multivessel ischemia, and complex culprit biology ( e . g ., large plaque burden) tend to benefit from a planned, staged, complete approach. Who might not? Older, frail patients or those with severe CKD, anemia, high bleeding risk, or tortuous/diffuse small-vessel disease may be better served with culprit-only PCI plus optimal medical therapy, reserving non-culprit revascularization for refractory symptoms or objective ischemia (opinion-based). In practice, a Heart Team-based, physiology-guided, staged strategy is most consistent with current guidance while we await a definitive NSTEMI-specific RCT [ 29 , 30 , 31 , 37 , 38 , 39 , 40 , 41 ].

When PCI is pursued in the NSTEMI setting, particularly for complex or multivessel disease, contemporary evidence increasingly supports the use of intravascular imaging (IVUS or OCT) to guide procedural decision-making [ 46 ]. This is a Class 1 recommendation in the 2025 ACS guidelines. Intravascular imaging can optimize stent sizing, characterize plaque morphology and composition, confirm adequate stent expansion and apposition, and detect complications such as edge dissection or tissue protrusion that may not be apparent on angiography alone. These modalities are particularly valuable in NSTEMI, where culprit lesion identification may be challenging, and in cases of suspected SCAD, when OCT is used selectively to distinguish dissection flaps from atherosclerotic disease [ 46 ].

5. Conclusion NSTEMI is a heterogeneous clinical syndrome that encompasses a spectrum of mechanisms, including atherothrombotic plaque disruption (rupture, erosion, and calcified nodules), dynamic epicardial or microvascular obstruction, spontaneous coronary artery dissection, thromboembolism, and supply–demand imbalance; each mechanism has distinct diagnostic pathways and therapeutic implications. Moving from a broad syndromic label to a personalized mechanism-specific diagnosis is imperative. In selected cases, standard evaluation may be insufficient, and more advanced diagnostic tools, if available, may be needed, as described in patients with MINOCA. However, in the vast majority of cases, good clinical judgment, along with standard diagnostic and therapeutic tools, should be sufficient to establish an appropriate diagnosis and guide effective treatment.

6. Future Developments For atherosclerotic disease and Type 1 MI, prevention is essential. Earlier detection and treatment of atherosclerosis are critical to significantly reduce Type 1 MI (both STEMI and NSTEMI). Clinicians should aim to identify at-risk patients earlier in the disease course through appropriate screening and risk-factor modification. Potential approaches include coronary artery calcium scoring and, ideally, CT angiography or other techniques in appropriately selected high-risk patients. CT angiography can identify asymptomatic plaque burden and plaque characteristics, particularly low-attenuation plaque. In the multicenter SCOT-HEART trial, low-attenuation noncalcified plaque burden on CCTA emerged as the strongest independent predictor of future fatal or nonfatal myocardial infarction, outperforming cardiovascular risk scores, coronary artery calcium scoring, and stenosis severity. Patients with low-attenuation plaque burden exceeding 4% had an almost 5-fold increased risk of subsequent MI [ 47 , 48 , 49 ]. A recent expert consensus statement from the Quantitative Cardiovascular Imaging Study Group provided evidence-based recommendations for integrating CCTA with artificial intelligence (AI)-supported plaque analysis to individualize treatment based on atherosclerotic plaque characterization, highlighting low-attenuation plaque and positive remodeling as key features for cardiovascular risk assessment [ 50 ].

Lifelong attention to modifiable risk factors, including hypertension, diet/exercise/obesity, low-density lipoprotein levels, avoidance of smoking/other pollutants, and glucose control (HbA1c) in patients with diabetes, is essential and should be a priority for anyone who values optimal cardiovascular health. Patients with a family history of premature myocardial infarction, stroke, or sudden death in adulthood should also have lipoprotein(a) measured. Recent guidelines recommend screening for atherosclerosis beginning at age 30 years, using the PREVENT Risk Calculator (refer clinicians to contemporary lipid and hypertension guidelines for additional recommendations) [ 51 ].

6.1 Artificial Intelligence in Diagnosis and Management AI holds considerable promise for earlier detection, more precise risk stratification, and improved imaging interpretation; however, AI also requires prospective validation, equitable performance across populations, and smooth integration into clinical workflows [ 52 , 53 , 54 , 55 ]. Potential applications include automated interpretation of symptoms and ECGs, serial biomarker testing to enable earlier diagnosis or safe early discharge, and AI-based plaque characterization using intravascular or noninvasive imaging [ 56 , 57 ]. Barriers to widespread clinical adoption include the need for robust external validation across diverse populations, integration into existing care pathways, clinician interpretability, and the risk of bias. Current guidelines acknowledge the promise of AI but stop short of recommending routine adoption. Ongoing prospective studies will determine whether AI improves actionable outcomes, including time to therapy, bleeding-adjusted net clinical benefit, and resource utilization [ 51 ].

6.2 Unanswered Questions 6.2.1 Plaque Erosion: A Distinct Mechanism Requiring Tailored Management Unlike plaque rupture, which involves disruption of a thin fibrous cap overlying a macrophage-infiltrated, lipid-rich necrotic core, plaque erosion is characterized by endothelial denudation over a proteoglycan- and smooth muscle cell-rich plaque without cap disruption. Moreover, plaque erosion is driven by innate immune mechanisms, including Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) activation, neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, and hyaluronan degradation, and results in a predominantly platelet-rich (white), nonocclusive thrombus [ 58 , 59 ]. Erosion accounts for approximately 25–40% of ACS cases in younger patients, women, and smokers with fewer traditional risk factors, and represents a majority of coronary thrombi in women under 50 years of age [ 60 ]. Currently, in addition to a healthy lifestyle, there is no consensus on strategies to prevent plaque erosion. Further studies are required.

6.2.2 Invasive Strategy in Type 2 NSTEMI Type 2 NSTEMI is associated with higher in-hospital and post-discharge mortality than Type 1 NSTEMI [ 14 ]. While patients with Type 2 NSTEMI have more comorbidities, current data do not establish CAD as the cause of the higher mortality. However, CAD is often present among patients undergoing invasive evaluation. These patients are routinely excluded from ACS intervention trials, leaving no randomized evidence to guide whether, when, or in whom angiography and/or revascularization should be performed. Observational data suggest that a subset of patients with underlying obstructive CAD may benefit from invasive evaluation once the inciting trigger is corrected, but reliably identifying this subgroup remains challenging [ 30 ]. Prospective trials are needed to determine which Type 2 NSTEMI patients warrant coronary angiography or revascularization, and to define the optimal timing relative to the precipitating condition.

6.2.3 Prasugrel Versus Ticagrelor Both prasugrel and ticagrelor are preferred over clopidogrel in ACS patients undergoing PCI, yet guidelines diverge in their recommendations. The 2023 ESC guidelines assign prasugrel a Class 2a preference based primarily on the open-label ISAR-REACT 5 trial, whereas the 2025 ACC/AHA guidelines consider prasugrel and ticagrelor interchangeable (Class 1), citing design limitations that constrain the generalizability of a single study [ 29 , 31 , 61 , 62 , 63 ]. Prasugrel remains contraindicated in patients with prior stroke/transient ischemic attack (TIA) and requires dose reduction in older or low-weight patients. In contrast, ticagrelor is the only potent P2Y12 inhibitor with Class 1 guideline support for medically managed NSTE-ACS without planned PCI [ 29 , 63 ]. A definitive double-anonymized head-to-head trial is still needed.

6.2.4 DAPT After Drug-Coated Balloon (DCB) Angioplasty DCBs deliver drugs without leaving a permanent scaffold. Trials such as BASKET-SMALL 2 and DEBUT support their efficacy in small-vessel disease and in patients at HBR [ 64 , 65 , 66 , 67 ]. One randomized trial demonstrated the non-inferiority of stepwise DAPT de-escalation compared with standard 12-month DAPT in ACS patients treated exclusively with DCB [ 68 ]. The International DCB Consensus Group endorses only 4 weeks of DAPT after DCB-only angioplasty. Nevertheless, current ESC guidelines still extrapolate longer DAPT durations from stent-based data, underscoring the need for larger confirmatory trials [ 31 , 64 ].

6.2.5 Updated Nomenclature for STEMI/NSTEMI? Over the years, the nomenclature for what one now refers to as NSTEMI has evolved. As outlined in the historical perspective, the original terminology was non-transmural MI. It then changed over time to subendocardial or non-Q-wave MI and finally NSTEMI. New data suggests that further evolution should be considered. It has been shown that NSTEMI with total coronary occlusion of the infarct-related artery has a worse prognosis than NSTEMI without total occlusion but similar to STEMI with total occlusion [ 69 ]. Thus, nomenclature should now reflect the presence of total occlusion as it provides a more accurate classification of STEMI/NSTEMI. However, the authors of this review do not necessarily concur that new terminology is required as in a large percentage of NSTEMI, one is unable to assign an infarct-related artery.

Background The term Yentl syndrome , coined by Bernadine Healy in 1991, refers to the disparities in the management of acute myocardial infarction between men and women. Using data from the Swiss nationwide AMIS Plus (Acute Myocardial Infarction in Switzerland) registry, we analyzed temporal trends of this sex gap.

Methods The AMIS Plus registry includes patients with acute myocardial infarction admitted to 84 Swiss hospitals. We analyzed sex differences in the use of percutaneous coronary intervention across 3 consecutive 6‐year periods (2007–2012, 2013–2018, 2019–2024), separately for ST‐segment–elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and non‐STEMI.

Results Between January 2007 and December 2024, a total of 48 357 patients were enrolled. Of these, 36 169 were men (74.8%) and 12 188 women (25.2%). STEMI and non‐STEMI comprised 57.6% and 42.4% of the population, respectively. Across all three 6‐year periods, men were more likely to undergo percutaneous coronary intervention for both STEMI and non‐STEMI ( P <0.001) than women. However, the sex gap narrowed significantly over time: in patients with STEMI from 8.8% (95% CI, 8.0%–9.6%) in 2007 through 2012, to 3.2% (95% CI, 2.7%–3.9%) in 2013 through 2018, and 2.7% (95% CI, 2.0%–3.5%) in 2019 through 2024, and in patients with non‐STEMI from 14.8% (95% CI, 13.8%–16.0%) to 6.3% (95% CI, 5.4%–7.2%) and 7.4% (95% CI, 6.2%–8.7%) over the same periods.

Conclusions In this nationwide prospective registry, we observed a marked reduction in sex‐related disparities in percutaneous coronary intervention use among patients with myocardial infarction in Switzerland from 2007 to 2024. These findings offer hope that the long shadow of the Yentl syndrome finally may be receding.

For Sources of Funding and Disclosures, see page 6. Nonstandard Abbreviation and Acronym AMIS Plus Acute Myocardial Infarction in Switzerland Clinical Perspective What Is New? Using data from the Swiss nationwide AMIS Plus (Acute Myocardial Infarction in Switzerland) registry, we observed a marked reduction in sex‐related disparities in the use of percutaneous coronary interventions in Switzerland from 2007 to 2024. The sex gap narrowed in patients with ST‐segment–elevation myocardial infarction from 8.8% (95% CI, 8.0%–9.6%) in 2007 to 2012, to 2.7% (95% CI, 2.0%–3.5%) in 2019 to 2024. What Are the Clinical Implications?

These findings suggest that sustained implementation of guideline‐based care and national quality initiatives can substantially reduce sex inequities in the management of acute myocardial infarction. Future initiatives should continue to focus on improving recognition, risk stratification, and timely invasive management of acute myocardial infarction in women. Dr Bernadine Healy coined the term Yentl syndrome in 1991 to call attention to the sex difference in the management of coronary artery disease (CAD). 1

The 2 trials in the same issue of the New England Journal of Medicine documented that for similar symptoms and signs of CAD, women were considerably less likely than men to undergo coronary angiography and revascularization. 2 , 3 However, once the diagnosis of severe CAD or myocardial infarction was established, women were as likely as men to undergo coronary angiography and revascularizations. As Healy put it in reference to “the Yentl syndrome at work”: “Once a woman showed that she was just like a man by having severe CAD, she was treated as a man would be.” 1

More than 3 decades later, the sex gap in the management of CAD remains conspicuous. Despite heart disease continuing to be the leading cause of death among women in the United States and worldwide, 4 numerous cross‐sectional and cohort studies showed that, compared with men, women with CAD still faced delays in diagnosis and revascularization. 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 While sex differences in the management of CAD have been extensively well documented, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood, and sex disparities in care seem to be in many places as pronounced today as they were in 1991.

To our knowledge, no data exist documenting the evolving pattern of the sex gap in the treatment of CAD. Our interest in the topic of the Yentl syndrome dates back to 1995. 11 Building on this, we used the nationwide AMIS Plus (Acute Myocardial Infarction in Switzerland) registry to analyze temporal trends in the management and outcomes of patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) between 2007 and 2024. 12 , 13 We paid particular attention to data highlighting the pattern of sex gaps in CAD care. METHODS Study Population The data that support the findings of this study are available from the AMIS Plus registry upon reasonable request ( ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT01305785 ).

AMIS Plus is a nationwide prospective registry endorsed in 1997 by the Swiss Societies of Internal Medicine, Cardiology, and Intensive Care, enrolling patients admitted with ACS in 84 hospitals ranging from community hospitals to large tertiary care facilities. 12 , 13 We included all patients admitted with ACS, who were enrolled between January 2007 and December 2024. ACS was diagnosed on the basis of clinical symptoms, ECG alterations, and elevations of cardiac enzymes according to current guidelines. 14

Myocardial infarction was defined by clinical symptoms, diagnostic pattern of biomarkers and subdivided on the basis of ECG characteristics into ST‐segment–elevation (STEMI) or non–ST‐segment–elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI).

Participating hospitals provided, on a voluntary basis, data in an anonymized fashion for each patient by the treating physician or a trained study nurse through standardized Internet‐based questionnaires to the AMIS Plus Data Center (located at Epidemiology, Biostatistics and Prevention Institute, University of Zurich, Switzerland). Additional external monitoring was performed in randomly selected hospitals using randomly selected cases to ensure data quality. Details of the registry have been described elsewhere. 12

Based on the number of patients treated for ACS in Swiss hospitals each year and the number of patients included in the registry, it is estimated that the cohort embraced 40% of all patients being treated for an ACS in the participating institutions and 20% of all patients being treated for an ACS in Switzerland during the investigated time period. All patients gave written informed consent to participate in the study. Data collection was conducted in accordance with the EU Note for Guidance on Good Clinical Practice CPMP/ECH/135/95 and the Declaration of Helsinki. The AMIS Plus registry was approved by the Swiss Supra‐Regional Ethics Committee for Clinical Studies, the Swiss Board for Data Security, and the Cantonal Ethics Commissions.

Data Collection Detailed clinical history including relevant comorbidities, vital status at admission, in‐hospital medical and interventional treatments, and morbidity and death during the in‐hospital period were assessed in all patients. Dyslipidemia, arterial hypertension, and diabetes were considered present if the patient was previously treated for these conditions or had it previously diagnosed. All in‐hospital medical treatments for ACS according to current guideline recommendations were assessed. 14 Time from admission to percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) that is, door‐to‐balloon time, was recorded.

Outcomes The main outcome of this study was differences in the use of PCI between women and men from 2007 to 2024. The secondary outcome was differences in the use of guideline‐recommended drug therapies in the same period.

Statistical Analysis First, we performed descriptive analyses according to three 6‐year time periods (2007–2012, 2013–2018, and 2019–2024) separate for patients with STEMI and NSTEMI. Second, we plotted a smoothed line curve based on the observed percentages of PCI use over time, along with the adjusted predicted probabilities of receiving PCI. The latter were estimated using logistic regression with a natural cubic spline for admission year to allow for nonlinear trends. The model included age, Charlson Comorbidity Index, Killip class, and delay from symptom onset to hospital admission as adjustment variables. 15

To allow for sex‐specific trends, an interaction between sex and the spline terms was included. The optimal number of knots in the spline was assessed by comparing the Akaike information criterion of models with 1 to 6 interior knots. Third, we performed logistic regression models for the use of PCI (ie, dependent variable) adjusted for age, Charlson Comorbidity Index, Killip class, and delay from symptom onset to hospital admission. Results are presented as odds ratios with 95% CIs. Categorical variables are presented as percentages and analyzed with the nonparametric Pearson χ 2 test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. Normally distributed continuous variables were expressed as means±SD and compared using the Student's 2‐tailed unpaired t test. Nonnormally distributed continuous variables are presented as medians with interquartile ranges and analyzed with the Mann–Whitney U test. All statistical tests were 2‐tailed. To prove robustness of the Mann–Whitney U test, we performed sensitivity analyses using Welch's t test for continuous variables, which did not materially alter the results. In the case of missing data, we provided n/N (number of patients with a characteristic/number of patients with available data) in all tables. No imputation method was used to complement missing data. A P value of <0.05 was considered significant. SPSS Statistics version 28 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY) was used for statistical analyses.

RESULTS Between January 2007 and December 2024, 48 357 patients, 74.8% men and 25.2% women, with acute myocardial infarction participated in the AMIS Plus cohort. Of these, 27 838 (57.6%) were diagnosed with STEMI and 20 519 (42.4%) with NSTEMI. An overview of the baseline characteristics is provided in Table S1 (patients with STEMI) and Table S2 (patients with NSTEMI). Women admitted with STEMI or NSTEMI were ≈10 years older than men, less often presented with typical pain, and less frequently were smokers but more often experienced dyspnea and had chronic comorbid conditions such as hypertension or diabetes.

PCI Use PCI use in men with STEMI (Table S3 ) slightly increased from 92.7% during the first 6‐year period (2007–2012) to 94.1% in the last 6‐year period (2019–2024), while in women the corresponding increase was from 83.9% to 91.4%. In men with NSTEMI (Table S4 ), the use of PCI decreased from 82.3% in the first 6‐year period to 81.2% in the last 6‐year period, while in women it increased from 67.5% to 73.8%. PCI use was higher ( P <0.001) for men with STEMI or NSTEMI as compared with women in all three 6‐year periods. In the overall cohort, the gap in the use of PCI between men and women decreased from 8.8% (95% CI, 8.0%–9.6%) between 2007 and 2012 to 3.2% (95% CI, 2.7%–3.9%) between 2013 and 2018, and to 2.7% (95% CI, 2.0%–3.5%) between 2019 and 2024 (Figure A ). In patients with NSTEMI, corresponding gaps were 14.8% (95% CI, 13.8%–16.0%), 6.3% (95% CI, 5.4%–7.2%), and 7.4% (95% CI, 6.2%–8.7%), respectively (Figure B ). Regression models showed that after adjustment for age, Charlson Comorbidity Index, Killip class, and delay from symptom onset to hospital admission, women with NSTEMI (odds ratio, 0.66 [95% CI, 0.53–0.81]; P <0.001) were still less likely to obtain PCI as compared with men in the last 6‐year period (2019–2024). In women with STEMI, the corresponding regression analysis for the same time period showed a nonsignificant trend toward less PCI use in women than in men (odds ratio, 0.75 [95% CI, 0.56–1.01]; P =0.06).

Door‐to‐Balloon Time of PCI In the first 6‐year period (2007–2012), the door‐to‐balloon time of PCI was significantly longer in women than in men ( P <0.001) with STEMI and NSTEMI (Tables S3 and S4 ). The difference between women and men in the door‐to‐balloon time of PCI decreased significantly ( P <0.001) from the first to the last 6‐year period from 8 to 4 minutes for patients with STEMI, and from 104 to 22 minutes for patients with NSTEMI. For patients with NSTEMI, the time difference between women and men was no longer significant in the last 6‐year period.

Use of Guideline‐Recommended Drug Therapies Most guideline‐recommended drug therapies were more frequently prescribed in male than in female patients with either STEMI or NSTEMI (Tables S3 and S4 ). For P2Y 12 inhibitors, a significant gap of 5.9% between male and female patients with STEMI in the first 6‐year period only slightly decreased to 4.0% in the last 6‐year period (Table S3 ); in patients with NSTEMI, the corresponding gap was 10.3% in the first and 5.6% in the last 6‐year period. Prescription rates for aspirin were high (>90%) for both men and women after STEMI or NSTEMI during all 6‐year periods but remained significantly ( P <0.001) higher for all time periods in men than in women.

DISCUSSION Our analysis of the prospective AMIS Plus registry revealed a reduction in the sex gap in the use of PCI among patients with acute myocardial infarction between 2007 and 2024. In patients presenting with STEMI, the sex gap in the use of PCI was no longer apparent after adjusting for women's older age at presentation and their higher burden of comorbidities. In those with NSTEMI, the sex gap in PCI use also narrowed over time; however, some disparity persisted through 2024. In the first 6‐year period, women presented with a higher risk pattern than men, including more frequent heart failure and diabetes and more severe CAD by Killip class. However, by 2024 these sex disparities had largely disappeared, indicating a convergence in clinical characteristics over time.

These findings beg the question of which factors contributed to the reduction of the sex gap. In this context, the marked improvement in door‐to‐balloon time, especially the greater shortening observed in women during the most recent 6‐year period compared with the earliest, may have facilitated this development. Among patients with NSTEMI, the sex gap in door‐to‐balloon time was completely eliminated, whereas in patients with STEMI, while it remained significant, it was reduced by 50%. The door‐to‐balloon time is a well‐known indicator of quality of care of patients with ACS and is determined by system‐related and hospital related factors. 16

Nearly 2 decades ago, Bradley et al outlined several strategies geared to reducing door‐to‐balloon time in acute myocardial infarction. 17 In Swiss tertiary care centers, the adoption of many of these measures may have helped achieve this goal, independent of sex. In addition to these measures, also patient‐related factors such as the delay between symptom onset and hospital admission may have contributed to the observed reduction of the sex gap. 18 , 19 Numerous studies have emphasized that timely reperfusion remains a cornerstone of improved survival in acute MI. 20 , 21 , 22

Experimental models documented a direct relationship between the duration of coronary artery occlusion and the extent of myocardial necrosis. 22 , 23 Myocardial cell death can begin as early as 20 minutes after occlusion and is typically complete within 6 hours. 23 Early reperfusion therapy significantly limits the extent of myocardial necrosis. Although delayed intervention may still offer some benefits, such as improved left ventricular remodeling and enhanced electrical stability, the most substantial advantage is achieved with prompt treatment. 16

Thus, the progressive narrowing of door‐to‐balloon time, together with the disappearance of baseline risk differences between women and men, contributed to the vanishing of the sex gap in PCI outcomes in Switzerland. Limitations First, acute ischemic heart disease with nonobstructed coronary arteries occurs considerably more often in women than in men. 24 Although by no means a benign entity, its clinical suspicion might delay door‐to‐needle time. Also, women and men with ACS have different clinical profiles, presentation, and outcomes, which may reflect sex differences in pathophysiology and anatomy. 25

Thus, despite all efforts, the sex gap is unlikely to vanish entirely. Second, data for this analysis originate from a country where access to PCI is universally available, independent of socioeconomic status or place of residence. Accordingly, the generalizability of these findings to settings where PCI access is constrained by socioeconomic disparities or limited by distance to the nearest catheterization laboratory may be restricted. Third, differences in PCI rates, particularly in NSTEMI, may reflect variation in underlying CAD rather than differential access to care alone. Residual confounding related to unmeasured angiographic and surgical variables cannot be excluded.

Conclusions Healy concludes her editorial with the hope “that the bold and charming heroine Yentl will survive, but that her syndrome will slip back into history as a curiosity of times gone by.” 1 Our study offers evidence that this is indeed taking place, at least in a small country like Switzerland, where equitable, and virtually unrestricted access to health care may have facilitated the vanishing of the sex gap in management of ACS. Background The European Society of Cardiology (ESC) 0/1h‐high‐sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs‐cTn)T/I‐algorithms have lower efficacy in patients with prior coronary artery bypass grafting. We hypothesized that in these high‐risk patients, the longer time to the second blood draw within the ESC 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms would increase efficacy, defined as the proportion of patients triaged to rule‐in/out of myocardial infarction, versus the ESC‐0/1h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms.

Methods In a prospective international multicenter diagnostic study including patients presenting to the emergency department with acute chest discomfort, final diagnoses were centrally adjudicated according to the Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction. Safety and efficacy of the guideline‐recommended ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms using assay‐specific use‐optimized cut‐offs were directly compared in patients with prior coronary artery bypass grafting. Findings were externally validated in an independent prospective US multicenter study.

Results Among 356 patients (median [interquartile range] age 73 [64–80] years, prevalence of non–ST‐segment–elevation myocardial infarction [NSTEMI]: 31% [n=112]), sensitivity for rule‐out of NSTEMI was high for the ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys‐algorithms (0/1h: 100% [95% CI 96.7–100]; 0/2h: Sensitivity: 99.1% [95% CI 95.1–99.8]). Specificity for rule‐in of NSTEMI was also high (0/1h: 97.1% [95% CI 94.2–98.6]; 0/2h 98.4% [95% CI 95.9–99.4]). Efficacy was 50.6% for 0/1h and 58.4% for 0/2h (difference: 7.9% [95% CI 4.2–11.5]). Findings with higher efficacy for 0/2h versus 0/1h were confirmed using hs‐cTnI‐Architect (difference in efficacy 3.1% [95% CI 0.1–6.1]) and using hs‐cTnI‐Atellica in the external validation cohort (n=178; difference in efficacy 9% [95% CI 4.5–13.5]).

Conclusions The ESC 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms have higher efficacy and comparable safety versus the ESC 0/1h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms in patients with prior coronary artery bypass grafting. Registration URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique Identifier: NCT00470587 .

Nonstandard Abbreviations and Acronyms ESC European Society of Cardiology hs‐cTn high‐sensitivity cardiac troponin hs‐cTnT/I high‐sensitivity cardiac troponin T/I NPV negative predictive value PPV positive predictive value Clinical Perspective What Is New?

In emergency department patients with prior coronary artery bypass grafting presenting with acute chest discomfort, the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) 0/2h‐high‐sensitivity cardiac troponin T/I (hs‐cTnT/I)‐algorithms increased efficacy versus the ESC 0/1h‐hs‐cTnT/I‐algorithms by triaging an additional 3% to 9% of patients to definitive rule‐out or rule‐in while maintaining very high safety and accuracy for non–ST‐segment–elevation myocardial infarction. What Are the Clinical Implications?

Using the ESC 0/2h‐hs‐cTnT/I‐algorithms in patients with prior coronary artery bypass grafting can modestly improve emergency department throughput by reducing the observe‐zone proportion without compromising rule‐out or rule‐in performance, but the workflow trade‐off of a longer sampling interval should be weighed against faster decision‐making with the ESC 0/1h‐hs‐cTnT/I‐algorithms. A pragmatic approach may be to apply the ESC 0/1h‐hs‐cTnT/I‐algorithms as the default strategy and obtain an additional 2‐hour sample for patients with coronary artery bypass grafting who remain in the observe zone to enable re‐triage using ESC 0/2h‐hs‐cTnT/I‐algorithms cutoffs.

In patients with complex coronary artery disease, the preferred treatment option is coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). 1 , 2 It is the most commonly performed cardiac surgical procedure, and due to demographic aging and improvements in secondary prevention, the number of patients with prior CABG is steadily increasing. 3 , 4 Because of their advanced coronary artery disease and multiple comorbidities, patients with prior CABG presenting with acute chest discomfort to the emergency department (ED) are at particularly high risk of experiencing a myocardial infarction (MI). 5 , 6

It is therefore concerning that all 3 diagnostic pillars in the early diagnosis of MI, that is, chest pain characteristics, the 12‐lead ECG, and high‐sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs‐cTn) T/I, have recently been shown to have lower diagnostic accuracy in patients with prior CABG. 5 , 7 , 8 While the safety of rule‐out and accuracy of rule‐in were maintained when applying the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) 0/1h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms, their efficacy, defined as the proportion of patients triaged to either definite rule‐out or rule‐in of MI, was lower in patients with prior CABG compared with those without, resulting in prolonged length of stay in the ED and increased resource utilization. 5 ,

7 , 8 Consequently, there is a major unmet clinical need to further improve early triage of high‐risk patients with prior CABG. In a post‐hoc analysis of 2 large prospective cohorts, we therefore performed a direct paired comparison of the ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTn algorithms, systematically quantifying differences in safety and efficacy and externally validating the findings, to test the hypothesis that extending the sampling interval to 2 hours may improve triage efficacy in patients with prior CABG by better differentiating frequent chronic hs‐cTn elevations from acute myocardial injury.

METHODS Study Design The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. This is a post hoc analysis from the APACE (Advantageous Predictors of Acute Coronary Syndromes Evaluation) study, enrolling consecutive adult patients presenting to the ED with acute chest discomfort ( ClinicalTrials.gov registry, number NCT00470587 ). 5 , 9

The central adjudication of the final diagnoses was performed by 2 independent cardiologists twice: once including serial measurements of hs‐cTnT (Elecsys, Roche Diagnostics) and once using hs‐cTnI (ARCHITECT STAT, Abbott Laboratories) in addition to all available clinical information including cardiac imaging, the local (hs)‐cTnT/I measurements, and study‐specific assessments including prospective assessment of 34 chest pain/discomfort characteristics and clinical follow‐up up to 90 days according to current guidelines and the fourth universal definition of MI. 10 , 11

To minimize a potential bias when directly comparing the performance of hs‐cTnT and hs‐cTnI based early triage algorithms in patients where the adjudicated diagnosis was either based on hs‐cTnT or hs‐cTnI, 2 independent adjudications were done to balance the effect of possibly diverging results for hs‐cTnT versus hs‐cTnI in favor of the hs‐cTn assay included in the central adjudication. 12 , 13 , 14

As the aim of the study was a direct comparison of the performance of the ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms in the same patients with prior CABG surgery, only patients with prior CABG and available hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys (analysis 1) and hs‐cTnI‐Architect (analysis 2) concentrations at presentation (0h), 1h and 2h were included. The 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes recommend excluding ST‐segment–elevation MI (STEMI) before applying the 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTn algorithms to rule‐out/in non–ST‐segment–elevation MI (NSTEMI). 10

We have therefore excluded patients with STEMI for this analysis. Furthermore, we excluded patients in whom the final diagnosis remained unclear (“unknown diagnosis”) even after central adjudication and in whom hs‐cTn concentrations were elevated, thereby possibly indicating MI. This small group of patients with cardiomyocyte injury reflects clinical reality where the reliable diagnosis or exclusion of MI is not feasible because of insufficient clinical work‐up and information. These patients were also excluded from all previous diagnostic analyses in the APACE trial (Figure 1 ). 7 , 8 , 15

Blood samples were collected at ED presentation (0 hour) and at 1, 2, 3, and 6 hours after presentation. Reporting is in accordance with the STARD statement (Table S1 ) and adheres to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Approval was obtained from local ethics committees, and all participants provided written informed consent. External Cohort Results were externally validated in the HIGH‐US using 0/1h‐and 0/2h‐hs‐cTnI‐Atellica‐algorithms. The methodology of the HIGH‐US study has been described in detail before. 17

In brief, adults aged 22 years and older who presented to the ED with any suspected acute MI prompting the clinical ordering of a cardiac troponin level test and who signed consent were prospectively enrolled in a Food and Drug Administration 510(k) study. The EDs were located in 29 centers across the United States in both tertiary urban settings and community hospitals. The adjudication panel consisted of cardiologists and emergency physicians, with 5 physicians (at least 2 members of each specialty) assigned to each case. These individuals and the treating emergency physicians were blinded to the hs‐cTnI results. Adjudicators determined acute MI diagnosis (both type 1 and type 2) with the Universal Definition of MI. Final diagnosis was determined by the majority adjudicator opinion.

17 Blood samples were scheduled at presentation (0h), after 1h (median time 57 minutes) and after 2.5h (median time 141 minutes) and the hs‐cTnI‐Atellica immunoassay (Siemens) was used. 8 , 17 Outcome The diagnostic outcome was an adjudicated diagnosis of index NSTEMI (type 1 or type 2). The prognostic outcome was all‐cause death at 30 and 730 days.

Objectives Primary objective was the direct comparison of the efficacy, defined as the proportion of patients triaged to definite rule‐out or rule‐in of MI by the ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms using hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys and hs‐cTnI‐Architect in patients with prior CABG. Secondary objective included comparison of the safety (defined as negative predictive value [NPV] and sensitivity) for rule‐out NSTEMI and accuracy (defined as positive predictive value [PPV] and specificity) for rule‐in NSTEMI as well as long‐term survival according to the classification of the ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms.
Statistical Analysis The ESC 0/1h‐and 0/2h‐hs‐cTn‐algorithms were applied using assay‐specific use‐optimized cut‐offs as recommended in current guidelines (Table 1 ). 18

We performed the analysis of the ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys‐algorithms (analysis 1) based on the adjudication including serial hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys measurements as part of the study specific data set. The performance of the ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTnI‐Architect‐algorithms (analysis 2) was based on a second independent adjudication including serial hs‐cTnI‐Architect (rather than hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys) measurements from the study samples as part of the study specific data set. NPV/sensitivity and PPV/specificity were derived from contingency tables comparing the algorithm‐based triage classification (rule‐out/observe/rule‐in) with the adjudicated index diagnosis of NSTEMI using the Wilson score method without continuity correction.

19 As NPV and PPV are prevalence‐dependent, we therefore also report sensitivity and specificity. Comparison of the efficacy, defined as the proportion of all patients triaged to definite rule‐out or rule‐in of MI, was calculated using the McNemar test. 20 Furthermore, we performed exploratory sensitivity analyses including type 1 MI only, in patients with renal dysfunction (defined as an estimated glomerular filtration rate <60 mL/min per 1.73 m 2 ) and in the elderly (≥70 years). 21 , 22 Table 1 Assay‐Specific Cutoffs for the European Society of Cardiology 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐Algorithms 0/1h‐algorithm Rule‐out Rule‐in Very low *

To provide clinically meaningful short‐ and long‐term prognosis and to enable comparability with prior studies reporting prognostic outcomes after application of ESC hs‐cTn algorithms, survival at 30 days and 730 days of follow‐up according to the classification provided by the ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐ hs‐cTn‐algorithms was plotted in Kaplan–Meier curves and the log‐rank test was used to assess differences in survival between groups without multivariable analyses. 23 , 24

Patients lost to follow‐up or alive at day 730 were right‐censored. Hazard ratios for all‐cause mortality at 730 days were estimated using multivariable Cox proportional hazards models with rule‐out as the reference category, adjusting for age, sex and estimated glomerular filtration rate.

For the analysis of the 0/1h‐and 0/2h‐hs‐cTnI‐Architect‐algorithms, 352 patients (median [IQR] age 73.0 [64.0, 80.0] years, 15% [n=53] women) with 104/352 (30%) having an NSTEMI were eligible. Performance of the ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐ hs‐ cTn ‐Algorithms The safety for rule‐out NSTEMI was very high with both algorithms (0/1h: Sensitivity: 100% [95% CI 96.7–100], NPV: 100% [95% CI 96.1–100]; 0/2h: Sensitivity: 99.1% [95% CI 95.1–99.8], NPV: 99.2% [95% CI 95.7–99.9]; Figure 2A and 2B ). PPV and specificity for rule‐in of NSTEMI were also high with 91.8% (95% CI 84.0–96.0) and 97.1% (95% CI 94.2–98.6) for the 0/1h‐ and 94.9% (95% CI 87.7–98.0) and 98.4% (95% CI 95.9–99.4) for the 0/2h‐hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys‐algorithm, respectively. Applying the 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys‐algorithms, 49.4% (n=176) and 41.6% (n=148) of the patients remained in the observe zone, resulting in an efficacy of 50.6% for 0/1h‐ and 58.4% for 0/2h‐hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys‐algorithm (difference: 7.9% [95% CI 4.2%–11.5%]; P <0.001; Figure 3 ). When applying the cutoffs for the 0/2h‐hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys‐algorithm in the 176 patients remaining in the observe zone using the 0/1h‐hs‐cTnT‐Elecsys‐algorithm, 33 (18.8%) and 4 (2.3%) patients were triaged to rule‐out and rule‐in, respectively.

The safety for rule‐out NSTEMI was very high in both algorithms (0/1h: Sensitivity: 100% [95% CI 96.4–100], NPV: 100% [95% CI 95.6–100]; 0/2h: Sensitivity: 100% [95% CI 96.4–100], NPV: 100% [95% CI 96.2–100]; Figure 2C and 2D ). When applying the cutoffs for the 0/2h‐hs‐cTnI‐Architect‐algorithm in the 167 patients remaining in the observe zone using the 0/1h‐hs‐cTnI‐Architect‐algorithm, 16 (9.6%) and 4 (2.4%) patients were triaged to rule‐out and rule‐in, respectively.

External Validation In 178 patients eligible in the external validation cohort (prevalence of NSTEMI: 31/178 [17%]), the 0/1h and 0/2h hs‐cTnI‐Atellica‐algorithms provided very high safety for rule‐out NSTEMI (0/1h: Sensitivity: 100% [95% CI 89.0–100], NPV: 100% [95% CI 92.6–100]; 0/2h: Sensitivity: 100% [95% CI 89.0–100], NPV: 100% [95% CI 94.2–100]; Figure 4A and 4B ). PPV and specificity for rule‐in of NSTEMI were 73.5% (95% CI 56.9–85.4) and 93.9% (95% CI 88.8–96.7) for the 0/1h‐ and 75.0% (95% CI 58.9–86.2) and 93.9% (95% CI 88.8–96.7) for the 0/2h‐hs‐cTnI‐Atellica‐algorithm, respectively. Applying the ESC 0/1h‐ and 0/2h‐hs‐cTnI‐Atellica‐algorithms, 53.9% (n=96) and 44.9% (n=80) of the patients remained in the observe zone resulting in an efficacy of 46.1% for 0/1h‐ and 55.1% for 0/2h‐algorithms (difference: 9% [95% CI 4.5%–13.5%]; P <0.001).
