1 Introduction Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of death worldwide. A recent analysis on the burden of CVD from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study showed that the number of patients with CVD in 2023 reached 626 million, with disability‐adjusted life years (DALYs) and deaths reaching 437 million and 19.2 million, respectively [ 1 ]. Atherosclerosis (AS) is the main pathophysiological driving factor of clinical CVD, and its formation may be the result of interactions among metabolic, immune and neural physiological systems [ 2 ]. Traditional treatment strategies, such as statins and proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitors, focus mainly on reducing blood lipid levels to control the progression of AS and have greatly advanced the treatment of CVDs. Despite the use of potent lipid‐lowering strategies, including novel drugs to reduce low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL‐C) to target levels, a certain proportion of patients still experience major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), indicating the presence of other residual cardiovascular risks [ 3 ]. Although treatments to reduce systemic inflammation have been proven to improve the prognosis of some CVDs, none of the current treatments can directly address the local and multifaceted pathological processes occurring in the arterial wall [ 4 ]. This suggests that the progression of AS is not only driven by the complex interactions of endothelial dysfunction (ED), lipid accumulation, and a continuous inflammatory cascade but also affected by nerves, immunity, and the gut microbiota. Against this background, the current treatment methods cannot completely address this residual risk [ 5 ]. As the understanding of the mechanism of AS has continued to improve, the current research direction has therefore shifted from traditional lipid‐lowering interventions to more precise multidimensional integration strategies, such as immune metabolic reprogramming, spatial‐level gene expression regulation, neuroimmune interactions, and the microbiome–vascular axis, with the goal of achieving precise intervention and personalized management of AS [ 6 , 7 ].

The concept of AS has undergone an evolution in the past century, from a disease caused by high‐cholesterol levels to a dynamic, multisystem inflammatory disease. In the early 20th century, Anitschkow reported that feeding rabbits a high‐cholesterol diet could lead to AS, which established the classic cholesterol theory [ 8 ]. At the end of the 20th century, Ross integrated these observations and proposed that “AS is an inflammatory disease” [ 9 ]. The CANTOS trial (2017) provided the first direct clinical evidence that targeting inflammation reduces cardiovascular events [ 10 ]. The past 5 years have brought considerable progress in understanding the mechanisms underlying AS, marked by several conceptual advances. First, the discovery of the neuroimmune–cardiovascular interface (NICI) showed that AS involves not only local vascular inflammation but also that the peripheral nervous system can interact with atherosclerotic intimal plaques through adventitial immune cells [ 2 ]. Second, the concept of trained immunity has reshaped the understanding of AS. Innate immune cells can obtain long‐term, highly reactive “memory” through metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming after exposure to atherogenic stimuli such as oxidized low‐density lipoprotein (ox‐LDL). Trained immunity therefore links transient metabolic stimuli to persistent vascular inflammation, which may explain the chronic progression of AS [ 11 ]. Third, single‐cell spatial transcriptomics, unlike traditional transcriptomics, resolves the spatial location of cells. In the past 2 years, through the integration of multiplatform analyses of human coronary and carotid plaques, the spatial distribution of immune cells and stromal cells, the cell neighborhood interaction network, and the differentiation trajectory of various cell subtypes in different regions of plaques have been found at the single‐cell level for the first time, providing a complex molecular map for explaining the local immune response and plaque heterogeneity of AS [ 12 , 13 ]. Fourth, the concept of the oral–gut–vascular axis has improved the understanding of the role of the oral and intestinal microbiome in AS. Studies have shown that the oral microbiome can directly translocate into the vascular wall to affect plaques and that the intestinal microbiota can also regulate the development of AS. On this basis, the oral–gut–vascular axis extends the view of AS beyond the vessel wall and identifies microbial targets for therapy [ 14 , 15 ]. Fifth, single‐cell technologies have clarified the contribution of adaptive immunity in AS. High‐resolution profiling has revealed clonal expansion, exhaustion, and effector differentiation in lesional T cells, along with the accumulation of age‐associated B cells and adventitial tertiary lymphoid structures, suggesting that adaptive immune circuits are attractive therapeutic targets [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ]. Sixth, clonal expansion has prompted a re‐evaluation of vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) involvement in plaque pathogenesis. Lineage‐tracing and single‐cell analyses have shown that a small pool of modulated VSMCs can undergo clonal outgrowth and eventually become a dominant cellular component of the lesion, a finding that challenges the conventional view of uniform phenotypic switching and reveals additional layers of plaque complexity [ 20 , 21 ]. AS is therefore best viewed as a multidimensional disease involving neuroimmune crosstalk, innate and adaptive immunity, metabolic reprogramming, the microbiome, and VSMC clonal dynamics.

This review focuses on recent mechanistic and conceptual updates in AS, particularly breakthroughs in trained immunity, adaptive immune regulation, VSMC plasticity, and the microbiome–vascular axis. On this basis, we discuss the current treatment strategies, emerging intervention methods and clinical trial progress and then analyze the key challenges and technical solutions involved in translating basic research into clinical research to provide a reference for future research directions in this field.

2 Pathogenesis: Canonical Concepts and Recent Advances AS is a chronic inflammatory disease driven by complex interactions among vascular dysfunction, lipid accumulation, immune activation, and cellular plasticity. The disease begins with ED and subendothelial lipoprotein retention, followed by monocyte recruitment, foam‐cell formation, VSMCs remodeling, and progressive plaque destabilization (Figure 1 ). Building on this pathological continuum, the following sections discuss the major molecular and cellular mechanisms of AS, with particular emphasis on recent advances in ED, lipid metabolic reprogramming, inflammatory cascades, VSMC plasticity, and the microbiome–vascular axis.

FIGURE 1 Initiation and progression of the atherogenic continuum. Disruptive stimuli first cause dysfunction in the endothelium, impairing its protective functions. This leads to leukocyte recruitment via adhesion molecules and chemokines. Recruited monocytes differentiate into macrophages, which take up trapped ox‐LDL via scavenger receptors to become foam cells. Finally, plaque remodeling involves VSMC migration, proliferation, and phenotypic switching, contributing to plaque development.

2.1 Endothelial Dysfunction 2.1.1 Hemodynamic Determinants and Molecular Pathogenesis ED is not merely a passive consequence of cardiovascular risk factors but also a central driver of AS, contributing to disease progression from lesion initiation to clinical manifestation [ 22 ]. Constitutive nitric oxide (NO) generation is one of several major protective mechanisms used by a healthy endothelium to preserve vascular integrity and control vascular homeostasis at baseline by maintaining vasodilation, preventing platelet aggregation, inhibiting the growth of VSMCs, and preventing the attachment of leukocytes to the vessel wall. This activity is supplemented by the activities of other mediators, such as prostacyclin and tight regulation of the renin–angiotensin system [ 23 ]. ED reflects a homeostatic imbalance initiated by injurious stimuli and fueled by a self‐perpetuating cycle of inflammation, oxidative stress, and progressive vascular damage. Hemodynamic forces are among the most important spatial determinants of endothelial injury. Atherosclerotic plaques preferentially develop at arterial sites exposed to disturbed, nonlaminar flow, such as at curvatures, bifurcations, and branch points. In contrast, high, atheroprotective laminar shear stress (LSS) produced by unidirectional laminar flow in straight, unbranched segments promotes a quiescent, anti‐inflammatory endothelial phenotype. Disturbed flow(DF), however, creates low‐magnitude, oscillatory shear stress (OSS) that inhibits endothelial gene expression and function, promoting a proadhesive, proliferative state. Thus, while systemic risk factors create a generalized proatherogenic milieu, the DF acts as a “localizing factor,” priming specific anatomic sites for initial lesion development [ 24 , 25 ].

Specialized mechanosensors, such as the junctional mechanosensory complex of PECAM‐1, VE‐cadherin, and VEGFR2 [ 26 ], along with other critical players, including specific integrins [ 27 ], the endothelial glycocalyx [ 28 ], various GPCRs [ 29 ], and the ion channel PIEZO1 [ 30 ], convert distinct shear stress patterns into intracellular biochemical signals on the endothelial cell surface (Figure 2 ). The role of PIEZO1 is highly context dependent: under protective LSS, it can activate signals that upregulate expression of mitochondrial SIRT4, which helps curb ox‐LDL uptake and oxidative stress [ 31 ], whereas under atherogenic OSS, it triggers a distinct Ca 2 + /calmodulin/CaMKII‐FAK/Src signaling cascade that leads to the activation and nuclear translocation of Yes‐associated protein (YAP) [ 32 , 33 ]. YAP, a key effector of the Hippo pathway, acts as a master transcriptional regulator, driving proinflammatory, proliferative, fibrotic, and senescence programs [ 34 , 35 ]. Its activation is intricately controlled by multiple additional pathways, including the MST1–connexin‐43 axis [ 36 ], phase‐separated DDR1 condensates [ 37 ], glycocalyx‐mediated CD44 signaling [ 38 ], and signaling through the serotonin receptor 5‐HT1B [ 39 ]. GPCRs also contribute in a context‐specific manner: for instance, GPR30 (GPER1) activation is considered atheroprotective, partly through the induction of Krüppel‐like factor 2 (KLF2) [ 40 ], whereas GPR68 [ 41 ] and G protein‐coupled receptor kinase 2 (GRK2) [ 42 ] propagate inflammatory signals. Recent additions to the repertoire of known mechanosensors include the redox‐regulated kinase TNIK [ 43 ] and the semaphorin receptor Plexin D1 [ 44 ].

FIGURE 2 Mechanotransduction pathways and cellular responses to shear stress in endothelial cells. Shear stress is sensed by endothelial membrane mechanosensors, including ion channels, GPCRs, integrins, the glycocalyx, BMP receptors, and the VE‐cadherin/VEGFR2/PECAM‐1 junctional complex. These mechanosensors activate intracellular signaling pathways that regulate nuclear transcription factors and downstream adhesion molecules and inflammatory mediators. The resulting transcriptional responses contribute to inflammation, oxidative stress, ER stress, apoptosis, pyroptosis, EndMT, autophagy, and proliferation, thereby influencing endothelial homeostasis and atherosclerosis progression.

Sustained ED is maintained through two interconnected processes: inflammatory signaling networks that drive acute endothelial activation and epigenetic reprogramming mechanisms that stabilize these pathological states over time. Among the inflammatory pathways, NF‐κB functions as a central hub linking disturbed‐flow signaling to maladaptive endothelial responses. The canonical pathway for NLRP3 inflammasome activation, a key driver of IL‐1β maturation, requires an NF‐κB‐dependent priming step (inducing NLRP3 and pro‐IL‐1β expression) and a second signal (e.g., lysosomal cathepsin B or mitochondrial reactive oxygen species [ROS]) that triggers the assembly of the inflammasome complex, leading to gasdermin D (GSDMD) pore formation, pyroptosis [ 45 ], and the release of mature IL‐1β [ 46 ]. Intriguingly, a noncanonical NF‐κB pathway (dependent on NIK and RelB) can directly upregulate GSDMD and caspase‐1 expression via interferon regulatory factor 1 (IRF‐1), bypassing the need for the NLRP3 sensor itself [ 47 ]. Organelle dysfunction sustains this cycle of inflammation. For example, S‐nitrosylation of the chaperone protein Hsp90 increases oxidative stress by impairing its ability to fold mitochondrial proteins and deal with ROS [ 48 ]; monoamine oxidase A (MAO‐A) and mtDNA leakage into the cytosol activate STING–PERK signaling in the endoplasmic reticulum, further integrating stress responses [ 49 , 50 ]. Furthermore, a subset of CD163 + macrophages can induce NF‐κB/Snail‐driven endothelial‐to‐mesenchymal transition (EndMT) in endothelial cells, which promotes the loss of endothelial identity and the acquisition of mesenchymal, profibrotic traits that lead to fibrous cap thinning and plaque vulnerability [ 51 ]. Collectively, these inflammatory and stress‐responsive pathways not only drive acute endothelial activation but also establish a permissive environment for more durable phenotypic alterations. In addition to acute inflammatory signaling, DF induces durable epigenetic reprogramming characterized by alterations in chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, DNA methylation, and noncoding RNA networks. Recent studies have demonstrated that AP‐1‐dependent chromatin remodeling [ 52 ], EZH2‐mediated H3K27me3 deposition [ 53 ], DNMT1‐driven DNA methylation [ 54 ], and lncRNA‐guided chromatin regulation [ 55 ] establish persistent endothelial phenotypes and provide a mechanistic basis for endothelial memory during atherogenesis. Among these regulatory mechanisms, noncoding RNAs have emerged as important modulators of endothelial phenotypic stability. Endothelial‐enriched microRNAs, particularly miR‐181a2b2 [ 56 ] and miR‐126 [ 57 ], are vital regulators of endothelial inflammation, apoptosis, and vascular homeostasis, further highlighting the contribution of noncoding RNA networks to endothelial phenotypic stability and atherogenesis.

2.1.2 Pathophysiology in Metabolic and Vascular Disease AS is a major macrovascular complication of diabetes, and ED serves as a central pathogenic link among hyperglycemia, metabolic dysfunction, and the development of diabetic vascular complications [ 58 , 59 ]. Youth‐onset type 2 diabetes, in which coronary ED appears early, provides supporting evidence. Plasma‐derived extracellular vesicles from these patients directly induce oxidative stress and endothelial inflammation, supporting their pathogenic role in early vascular dysfunction [ 60 ]. Endothelial homeostasis is tightly maintained by a delicate balance of transcriptional and metabolic regulators, which is often disturbed under hyperglycemic conditions. For instance, the transcription factor KLF11 acts as an important gatekeeper, hindering TXNIP‐induced oxidative stress and blocking Notch1/Snail‐mediated EndMT [ 61 ]. Hyperglycemia induces persistent alterations in endothelial phenotypes through multilayered epigenetic modifications. In human aortic endothelial cells, high glucose levels upregulate expression of EZH2 to increase repressive H3K27me3 deposition at antioxidant promoters (SOD and JunD), driving oxidative stress and downstream NF‐κB activation [ 62 ]. Simultaneously, metabolic lactate accumulation induces protein lactylation; specifically, IDH2 lactylation at K272 alters the Cav1–eNOS interaction to regulate endothelial eNOS activity and angiogenesis under diabetic conditions [ 63 ]. These epigenetic changes offer direct therapeutic targets. The bromodomain and extraterminal inhibitor apabetalone reverses pathological epigenetic memory via the BRD4/P300/H3K27ac axis, thereby suppressing NLRP3 inflammasome‐mediated endothelial pyroptosis [ 64 , 65 ] and restoring ABCA1‐dependent cholesterol metabolism [ 66 ]. These alterations are further reinforced at the posttranscriptional level through dysregulated noncoding RNA networks. Under diabetic stress, the downregulated expression of endothelial miR‐126 derepresses SPRED1, dampening MAPK signaling, and eNOS expression [ 67 ]. Furthermore, hyperglycemia depletes functional miR‐126 from endothelial microparticles (EMPs), abolishing their cell‐to‐cell reparative capacity, a defect directly confirmed in circulating microparticles of diabetic patients with vascular diseases [ 68 ].

Apart from metabolic insults, one of the main causes of ED is hemodynamic stress in the form of hypertension, which accelerates the development of AS. Hypertension‐driven ED is mediated through numerous synergistic pathways. Ang II selectively damages endothelium‐dependent dilation in coronary arteries and suppresses protective prostaglandin biosynthesis [ 69 ]. At the same time, organelle homeostasis is disturbed by hypertensive stress: impaired iron export via ABCB8 causes mitochondrial dysfunction, which initiates an iron‐dependent TGF‐β signaling axis that drives oxidative stress and inflammation [ 70 ]. Pressure overload activates proinflammatory adhesion molecules by upregulating expression of the endoplasmic reticulum protein Nogo‐B, facilitating ER–mitochondrial coupling via Mfn2 to increase calcium flux and ROS production [ 71 ].

2.2 Lipid Metabolism Reprogramming 2.2.1 The Concept of Lipid Metabolism Reprogramming The formation of foam cells is no longer regarded as a simple process of passive lipid overflow due to excessive lipoprotein uptake. It is now clear that plaque macrophages undergo reprogramming of intracellular cholesterol and fatty acid metabolism in response to local microenvironmental cues, thereby acquiring a persistent proinflammatory phenotype [ 72 , 73 ]. These environmental cues are crucially translated into long‐term metabolic programs by epigenetic regulators. For example, the histone demethylase KDM2A stimulates the Src family kinase FYN, creating a signaling axis that favors sustained lipid accumulation and inflammation [ 74 ]; conversely, the dephosphorylation of the nuclear receptor LXRα causes macrophages to switch to an anti‐inflammatory state that enables cholesterol excretion [ 75 ]. Lipid metabolites themselves can act as powerful signaling molecules: oxysterol 25‐hydroxycholesterol increases inflammation and TLR4/NF‐κB activation [ 76 ]. However, some proresolving lipid mediators, such as resolvin T4, can increase cholesterol efflux through the SR‐BI scavenger receptor, thereby facilitating the resolution of inflammation [ 77 ]. Membrane‐level nanoscale organization is equally important: agonism of the receptor TREM2 improves cellular cholesterol handling and collagen deposition, which increases plaque stability [ 78 ]. Moreover, the formation of specific cholesterol‐rich membrane microdomains called “inflammarafts” in nonfoamy macrophages provides hyperinflammatory platforms for the assembly and activation of Toll‐like receptors [ 79 ]. This metabolic reprogramming may be reversible. For example, in aged mice, blocking the prostaglandin E2 (PGE 2 )–EP2 receptor axis can restore myeloid cell bioenergetics and even reverse age‐associated cognitive decline [ 80 ]. Systemic metabolic interference also shows promise, as evidenced by studies demonstrating that hepatocyte‐specific deletion of the nuclear receptor corepressor NCOR1 reroutes bile acid metabolism, increases fecal sterol excretion, and significantly reduces AS in mice [ 81 ]. These findings suggest an expanding therapeutic focus that includes reprogramming myeloid cell metabolism and function within plaques alongside lowering circulating lipids.

2.2.2 Cholesterol Metabolism Through a variety of scavenger receptors, macrophages internalize aggregated lipoprotein particles and modified LDL (SRA, CD36, SR‐BI, LOX‐1, and LRP1) [ 72 ]. In addition to receptor‐mediated endocytosis, Nox2‐derived ROS stimulate nonspecific, receptor‐independent fluid‐phase macropinocytosis under hypercholesterolemic conditions, which contributes to the formation of foam cells even in response to native LDL [ 82 ]. Posttranslational regulation of scavenger receptors further influences the extent of modified lipid uptake. In particular, Lys63‐linked polyubiquitination of SR‐BI is catalyzed by the E3 ubiquitin ligase RNF128, which prevents lysosomal degradation and promotes recycling to the plasma membrane, thereby maintaining ox‐LDL uptake and inflammatory activation [ 83 ]. Once internalized, lipid overload dramatically alters the metabolism and function of macrophages. Downregulation of miR‐369‐3p expression hinders this adaptation in diabetic conditions by derepressing its target, the succinate receptor GPR91. This leads to increased oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), increased inflammasome‐driven inflammation, and worsened succinate signaling [ 84 ].

Unlike LDL, which has a well‐established proatherogenic role, high‐density lipoprotein (HDL) exerts context‐dependent effects and may lose its atheroprotective properties under pathological conditions. Importantly, its function can be positively regulated, as exemplified by hepatic ATF3, which increases HDL uptake via SR‐BI to promote reverse cholesterol transport and attenuate AS [ 85 ]. Paradoxically, high levels of HDL‐cholesterol (HDL‐C) are linked to increased atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk [ 86 ]. This may be because, under such conditions, HDL is more susceptible to oxidative modifications, which severely compromise its antiatherogenic properties [ 86 , 87 ].

2.2.3 Fatty Acid Metabolism Fatty acid metabolism is another critical component of metabolic reprogramming in AS. Fatty acid oxidation (FAO) plays a dual role in the disease process by regulating macrophage polarization and NLRP3 inflammasome activation, whereas adenosine 5′‐monophosphate‐activated protein kinase (AMPK) and peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor (PPAR) signaling are the key nodes that regulate FAO [ 88 ]. For example, docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) promotes macrophage polarization toward an anti‐inflammatory M2 phenotype and increases lipid metabolism and cholesterol efflux by activating PPAR signaling, a mechanism consistent with the upregulation of PPARα expression by macrophage angiotensin‐converting enzyme (ACE), which further increases FAO [ 89 , 90 ].

2.3 Inflammatory Cascades 2.3.1 Innate Immunity Plaque macrophages defy the traditional simple M1 (proinflammatory)/M2 (anti‐inflammatory/reparative) classification. High‐resolution single‐cell transcriptomic profiling has shown a continuous spectrum of distinct subtypes and states, including classical inflammatory cells that produce IL‐1β and TNF, TREM2 + lipid‐associated foam cells that, despite a homeostatic signature, can adopt proinflammatory roles through integration with signals such as GRN122, and newly identified populations such as apoptotic macrophages, SLAMF9 + macrophages, and FCGBP + macrophages, with the latter two potentially being involved in tissue repair and containment functions [ 91 , 92 , 93 , 94 ]. Functional validation is crucial, going beyond simple descriptive cataloging. Specifically, Lp(a)‐associated diacylglycerols promote macrophage priming via the TLR4/NF‐κB pathway and subsequent NLRP3 inflammasome activation, driving robust IL‐1β secretion. This dual‐signal mechanism correlates with the enrichment of distinct CD68 + CASP1 + IL‐1B + SELL + inflammatory and CD68 + IL‐18 + TLR4 + TREM2 + resident macrophage populations within human atherosclerotic plaques [ 95 ]. Concurrently, TLR4/MyD88/NF‐κB‐driven NLRP3 activation culminates in multiple forms of inflammatory cell death, including pyroptosis, apoptosis, and necroptosis [ 96 ]. Mendelian randomization, combined with direct analyses of human tissues, has identified macrophage‐derived lysosomal acid lipase (LIPA) as a potential causal driver of coronary artery disease (CAD) [ 97 ]. Dendritic cells (DCs) comprise several major subsets, including cDC1s, cDC2s, and pDCs, which are professional antigen‐presenting cells that take up arterial‐wall antigens (such as peptides derived from ApoB100) and are essential for initiating and directing the adaptive immune response. Different subsets of DCs frequently have conflicting effects on the course of disease [ 98 ]. Beyond macrophages and DCs, neutrophils actively contribute to plaque progression through the formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). Increasing evidence indicates that NETs function as potent amplifiers of vascular inflammation [ 99 ]. Mechanistically, cholesterol‐loaded macrophages promote NET formation through NLRP3 inflammasome‐dependent IL‐1β secretion, establishing a pathogenic macrophage–neutrophil inflammatory circuit [ 100 ]. NET‐associated histones further facilitate monocyte adhesion and accumulation within the arterial wall, thereby accelerating lesion growth [ 101 ]. In addition, NET formation is associated with increased local IL‐1β production and inflammatory cell recruitment within plaques, contributing to lesion progression [ 102 ]. Innate immune cells can also develop a de facto memory response known as “trained immunity” [ 103 ]. Rather than representing a transient activation, this process is maintained through coordinated metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming of hematopoietic progenitors and their myeloid descendants. In diabetes, transient hyperglycemia induces persistent chromatin remodeling and Runx1‐dependent inflammatory priming that remains detectable even after normalization of glucose levels, providing a mechanistic basis for metabolic memory and sustained vascular inflammation [ 104 ]. Likewise, ox‐LDL promotes trained immunity through metabolic rewiring, including increased mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, which drives long‐term inflammatory responsiveness [ 105 ]. Mechanistically, the oxysterol receptor LXRα links these metabolic alterations to epigenetic remodeling by regulating the activation of histone marks at inflammatory gene loci [ 106 ]. These findings highlight trained immunity as a central mechanism connecting metabolic stress, epigenetic memory, and persistent vascular inflammation in AS.

2.3.2 Adaptive Immunity T and B lymphocytes both play complex, precisely calibrated roles in the regulation of AS (Figure 3 ). Helper T type 1 cells (Th1s) and type 17 cells (Th17s) primarily have a proatherosclerotic effect, and some B2 cell‐derived antibodies are also similar according to well‐established experimental mouse models. Th2s, regulatory T cells (Tregs), and other innate B1 cells that produce natural IgM antibodies typically provide protection. Follicular helper T cells (Tfhs) located in lymphoid organs coordinate the antibody class switching of B cells and affect the quality of the humoral response [ 107 ]. However, cross‐species comparative single‐cell RNA‐seq analyses highlight significant distinctions between human disease and mouse models. Human plaques are rich in T cells, display clear signatures of IFN‐γ production and T‐cell exhaustion (a state of dysfunction in chronic antigen exposure), and exhibit persistent clonal expansion of CD4 + T cells that are specific for ApoB (the core protein of LDL) but resist neat classification into classical Th1, Th2, or Th17 subsets [ 108 , 109 ]. Recent single‐cell T‐cell receptor sequencing (scTCR‐seq) has characterized this clonal expansion as a breakdown of peripheral tolerance, supporting the concept that autoimmune mechanisms contribute substantially to AS progression [ 19 , 110 ]. As a prime example of this plasticity, seminal studies identifying specific ApoB epitopes (such as p18) reveal that these antigens primarily induce protective Foxp3 + regulatory T cells in healthy individuals [ 111 ]. However, these ApoB‐reactive CD4 + T cells progressively convert from initially protective Tregs to pathogenic, mixed‐phenotype effector cells during disease progression [ 112 ]. This pathogenic transition is further exemplified by the emergence of an unusual subset of CCR5 + T‐bet + Foxp3 + effector T cells, which utilize CCR5 to home specifically to the atherosclerotic aorta and drive AS rather than act as suppressors [ 113 ]. Along this line, the humoral response is correspondingly engaged, as anti‐ApoB autoantibodies exhibit distinct IgG‐ and IgM‐associated immune signatures, further supporting the autoimmune nature of AS [ 114 ]. Furthermore, this localized autoimmune response is amplified by molecular mimicry, in which expanded plaque TCRs cross‐react with both viral epitopes and resident vascular self‐antigens [ 115 ]. It is also believed that local cDC1s in plaques increase this autoinflammatory reaction by activating Th1 and CD8 T cells in a STING‐dependent manner [ 116 ]. The subsequent recruitment of these diverse immune cells into the inflamed vasculature is actively governed by cell type‐specific mechanisms; the CD40–CD40L axis has recently been demonstrated to drive this process, with endothelial‐expressed CD40L serving as a critical proatherogenic adhesion receptor for leukocytes [ 117 ]. Moreover, remote systemic events such as myocardial infarction (MI) can trigger the release of alarmins (e.g., IL‐1α and MRP8/14), activating B cells to generate pathogenic IgG antibodies that target neoantigens in the plaque [ 118 ]. Protective immunity can be dampened by the plaque microenvironment itself. For example, dysregulated glycolytic metabolism in human plaques impairs the function of infiltrating naïve CD4 + T cells, limiting their ability to mount effective regulatory responses [ 119 ]. Whether these human‐specific immune features reflect fundamental biological differences or simply differences in disease stage between human studies and experimental models remains an important question.

2.4 Vascular Smooth Muscle Cell Plasticity Recent advances in single‐cell and chromatin accessibility profiling have transformed our understanding of VSMC plasticity. The field has moved beyond isolated markers to explore complex spatiotemporal trajectories. The single‐nucleus assay for transposase‐accessible chromatin with sequencing (snATAC‐seq) across human coronary arteries has recently mapped over 320,000 accessible sites, identifying critical regulatory elements specifically within smooth muscle cell (SMC) transition states, such as fibromyocytes [ 120 ]. Concurrently, bioinformatic deconvolution of bulk microarrays using plaque scRNA‐seq data has highlighted multiple mesenchymal cell populations in atherosclerotic lesions, including distinct classical and modulated SMC subphenotypes [ 121 ]. These technologies reveal that the transition of VSMCs involves not only a loss of the contractile state but also a hyperproliferative process. Indeed, lineage tracing has demonstrated that SMC‐derived cells in AS exhibit tumor cell‐like characteristics, including genomic instability, evasion of senescence, and hyperproliferation, a phenotypic switch that can be accelerated by oncogenic mutations such as KrasG12D [ 21 ].

These lineage transitions are orchestrated by a multilayered epigenetic regulatory network. Traditionally, the protein arginine methyltransferase PRMT1 helps epigenetically maintain myocardin expression and the differentiated, contractile state [ 122 ]. However, under pathogenic stress, multilayered chromatin remodeling overrides this baseline. Recent single‐nucleus profiling has suggested PRDM16 as a key transcription factor driver in this process [ 120 ]. PRDM16 functions as a critical transcriptional repressor of the synthetic SMC phenotype by occupying chromatin and suppressing activating marks at synthetic loci; its deletion induces a synthetic program across all SMC subtypes [ 123 ]. Conversely, the histone methyltransferase SUV39H1 actively drives dedifferentiation by regulating dynamic trimethylation at histone H3 lysine 9 (H3K9me3), which alters chromatin accessibility and promotes the expression of KLF4 [ 124 ]. Furthermore, epigenetic regulation extends to noncoding regions, where the human‐specific long noncoding RNA INKILN physically interacts with and stabilizes MKL1 and USP10 to activate a proinflammatory gene program in VSMCs [ 125 ].

Ultimately, VSMCs differentiate into distinct phenotypes with opposing consequences for plaque fate through intricate microenvironmental crosstalk (Table 1 ). A classic two‐step conversion is triggered by high‐lipid stress and inactivation of the NOTCH pathway. First, VSMCs adopt a dedifferentiated “modulated” state, and subsequently, phagocytic, macrophage‐like cells that contribute to the necrotic core [ 126 ]. Recent single‐cell transcriptome data from human plaques corroborate this finding, showing that expression of the ChemR23 receptor is highest in contractile VSMCs but markedly reduced in synthetic ones and that its deficiency actively promotes the switching of VSMCs into macrophage‐like foam cells [ 127 ]. The transcription factor HOXA1 has been shown to accelerate this adverse change by upregulating expression of KLF4 and increasing NF‐κB p65 signaling [ 126 , 128 ]. In contrast, cells in intermediate differentiation states attempt to communicate with and stabilize the matrix; for example, the matricellular protein CCN2 can reduce ER stress and lipid uptake, promoting a more stable plaque phenotype [ 129 ]. Additionally, novel regulators, such as the circadian rhythm gene ARNTL, have been identified through transcriptomics; silencing ARNTL in human carotid SMCs attenuates proliferation and increases the expression of contractile markers [ 121 ]. As a result, plaque vulnerability is dictated by the dynamic equilibrium between these diverse, epigenetically driven fates.

John Wiley & Sons, Ltd. 2.5 Microbiome–Vascular Axis An increasing body of literature indicates that the gut and oral microbiomes serve as a “microbiome–vascular axis” in AS. Dysbiosis of the gut, characterized by an increased abundance of oral‐associated or even pathogenic bacteria (e.g., Streptococcus and Enterobacteriaceae ) and a low abundance of beneficial short‐chain fatty acid‐producing genera (e.g., Bacteroides ), is commonly observed in patients with CVDs. These microbes produce proatherogenic metabolites, most notably trimethylamine‐N‐oxide (TMAO), from dietary choline and L‐carnitine, as well as endotoxins such as lipopolysaccharide (LPS). They also systemically modulate host gene expression programs related to oxidative stress and DNA repair [ 130 , 131 ]. These microbial metabolites and endotoxins promote ED, activate the NLRP3 inflammasome and NF‐κB signaling in macrophages, and increase platelet reactivity and thrombotic risk [ 132 , 133 , 134 , 135 , 136 ]. The oral microbiome may also influence the microbiome–vascular axis independently of the gut microbiome. Oral bacterial species are enriched in the gut microbiota of patients with CVD. In particular, the periodontal pathogen Porphyromonas gingivalis may increase plasma TMAO levels by upregulating the expression of hepatic flavin‐containing monooxygenase 3 (FMO3) without necessarily altering gut microbial trimethylamine (TMA) production. These findings support the existence of an oral–liver–TMAO pathway that links oral health to systemic cardiovascular risk [ 137 , 138 ]. Nonetheless, the pathogenic effect of this loop appears to be quantitative rather than absolute. For example, in a large prospective cohort of vegetarian adults with chronically low TMAO levels, Tong et al. [ 139 ] reported a significant incidence of ischemic heart disease over 18 years of follow‐up, with a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.78 compared with that of the meat eaters. This implies that even with an attenuation of the TMAO axis, there is an approximately 22% reduction in relative risk. These findings support three conclusions: (i) Platelet priming, among other biological activities, can be preserved even when patients are exposed to very little TMAO; (ii) This considerable remaining risk may be attributable to TMAO‐independent mechanisms, including Lp(a), clonal hematopoiesis, and vascular calcification, making interventions against TMAO additive but not curative; and (iii) TMAO is not a binary trigger but rather a continuous risk rheostat. Combined targeting of microbial TMA formation and these orthogonal pathways will thus probably be needed to minimize residual ASCVD risk.

3 Therapeutic Interventions Actively treating various proatherosclerotic conditions is an important strategy for preventing ASCVD events. For example, intensive lipid lowering, strict blood pressure control, and glycemic control can inhibit the progression of AS. Beyond diagnosing and treating the clinical manifestations of AS, clinicians must also manage the diseases and risk factors that promote AS, including lipid management, inflammation control, and immune modulation.

3.1 Current Therapeutic Interventions 3.1.1 Lifestyle Interventions Lifestyle interventions are the cornerstone of both primary and secondary prevention of AS, a point emphasized by all major guidelines. Although their importance is widely recognized, their actual implementation still requires improvement [ 140 ].

3.1.1.1 Dietary Modification Improving dietary habits is among the key nonpharmacological methods for preventing and managing CVD [ 140 ]. Studies emphasize reducing the intake of saturated fats and sodium while increasing the consumption of unsaturated fats, dietary fiber, fruits, vegetables, and whole grains [ 141 ]. In accordance with the American Heart Association's (AHA) “Life's Essential 8” guidelines, diet modification is among the key metrics for lowering ASCVD risk [ 142 ].

3.1.1.2 Physical Activity Physical activity is essential for cardiovascular health [ 143 ]. It is recommended to engage in at least 150 min of moderate‐intensity aerobic exercise per week, such as brisk walking, jogging, or swimming, and to incorporate strength training. Regular physical activity can improve cardiopulmonary function, aid in weight management, and positively impact blood pressure control [ 144 ]. Studies have shown that both aerobic exercise and strength training are effective at supporting cardiovascular risk‐factor management and are associated with a lower risk of all‐cause mortality [ 143 ].

3.1.1.3 Smoking Cessation and Alcohol Restriction Smoking is an important and modifiable risk factor for AS. AHA guidelines emphasize smoking cessation as one of the key lifestyle metrics for reducing ASCVD risk. In addition, alcohol intake should be limited, as excessive consumption is associated with increased cardiovascular risk [ 140 ]. 3.1.1.4 Stress Management Chronic stress is one of the risk factors for CVD. Relaxation techniques such as meditation, yoga, and deep breathing can effectively alleviate mental stress, thereby maintaining a positive mindset. These psychological and social interventions are considered to be closely related to cardiovascular protection [ 140 ].

3.1.2 Pharmacological Treatment Pharmaceuticals play important roles in managing AS, controlling risk factors, maintaining plaque stability, and preventing major cardiovascular events (Table S1 ). 3.1.2.1 Lipid‐Lowering Drugs 3.1.2.1.1 Statins Statins are the cornerstone drugs for lowering LDL‐C levels, as they inhibit HMG‐CoA reductase to reduce cholesterol synthesis. They not only lower LDL‐C but also stabilize atherosclerotic plaques and exert anti‐inflammatory effects [ 145 ].

3.1.2.1.2 Cholesterol Absorption Inhibitors Inhibitors such as ezetimibe lower LDL‐C by inhibiting intestinal cholesterol absorption and are often used in combination with statins, especially for patients who cannot achieve LDL‐C targets with statin monotherapy [ 146 ].

3.1.2.1.3 Monoclonal Antibodies (mAbs) Against PCSK9 These drugs lower LDL‐C levels by inhibiting the ability of the PCSK9 protein to degrade LDL receptors, thereby increasing hepatic clearance of LDL‐C. They can not only effectively reduce LDL‐C levels by 50%–60% on the basis of statins and improve the prognosis of ASCVD patients [ 145 ] but also show benefits in primary prevention in high‐risk groups without a history of MI or stroke [ 147 ].

3.1.2.1.4 Small Interfering RNA (siRNA) Targeting PCSK9 The ORION clinical trial found a significant reduction in LDL‐C (50%) by inclisiran in patients with atherosclerotic CVD [ 148 ]. In addition, one study showed that after 3 months of inclisiran therapy, patients at high cardiovascular risk experienced significant reductions in LDL‐C levels and key inflammatory markers (PTX3 and IL‐18), suggesting that the drug has anti‐inflammatory effects beyond its lipid‐lowering effects [ 149 ]. A recent study evaluated the effect of inclisiran on plaque delipidation at the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) 2025 conference and found that maximum lipid‐core burden index at 4 mm was reduced in the inclisiran group from 193.7 to 103.2, a decrease of 46.7% (−90.5, p = 0.017) at the 15‐month follow‐up [ 150 ]. These findings indicate that inclisiran has the potential to stabilize plaques, and we look forward to more clinical studies to confirm these findings.

3.1.2.1.5 A Third‐Generation Small Binding Protein Targeting PCSK9 Lerodalcibep is a novel, third‐generation PCSK9 inhibitor based on an adnectin scaffold—a small binding protein engineered to bind with high affinity to human PCSK9. In one randomized, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled Phase 3 trial, 922 patients with established CVD or at very high or high CVD risk and LDL‐C ≥ 70 mg/dL (CVD) or ≥ 100 mg/dL (high risk) despite maximally tolerated statin therapy were randomized 2:1 to receive monthly subcutaneous lerodalcibep (300 mg) or placebo for 52 weeks. The percent change in LDL‐C at Week 52 showed a placebo‐adjusted LDL‐C reduction of 56.2%; 90% of lerodalcibep‐treated patients achieved ≥ 50% LDL‐C lowering and guideline‐recommended targets. Treatment‐emergent adverse events were similar between groups except for mild/moderate injection‐site reactions (6.9% vs. 0.3%). Therefore, monthly administration of lerodalcibep significantly reduced LDL‐C levels in high‐risk CVD patients, with a safety profile similar to that of placebo, supporting its long‐term use when statins alone are insufficient [ 151 ].

3.1.2.1.6 mAbs Against Angiopoietin‐Like Protein 3 (ANGPTL3) ANGPTL3, a protein predominantly synthesized by hepatocytes and secreted into the bloodstream, plays a key role in lipid metabolism by suppressing lipoprotein lipase and endothelial lipase activity, which in turn impedes the catabolism of triglyceride (TG)‐rich lipoproteins. Conversely, inherited deficiency variants of ANGPTL3 correlate with reduced plasma TG and LDL‐C concentrations, thereby lowering susceptibility to ASCVD [ 152 ]. Evinacumab is a human‐derived mAb specifically designed to target circulating ANGPTL3 protein. Clinical trials have shown that evinacumab significantly reduced LDL‐C levels by 42% from baseline at Week 24 in patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HoFH) [ 153 ] and significantly reduced LDL‐C levels by up to 56.0% at Week 16 in patients with refractory hypercholesterolemia [ 154 ]. In addition, evinacumab significantly reduced cardiovascular events over 4 years of follow‐up in patients with HoFH [ 155 ]. Recently, another mAb against ANGPTL3, SHR‐1918, resulted in a decrease in LDL‐C of 21.7%–29.9% among patients with moderate‐to‐high ASCVD risk in a Phase 2 study [ 156 ]. Furthermore, in a Phase 1 trial involving 48 adults with mixed hyperlipidemia, LY3475766—a human mAb specifically blocking ANGPTL3/8—was well tolerated and dose‐dependently reduced TG (up to −70%), remnant cholesterol (−86%), and LDL‐C (−32%) while increasing HDL‐C (+27%) levels [ 157 ].

3.1.2.1.7 mAbs Against Angiopoietin‐Like Protein 4 (ANGPTL4) ANGPTL4 is a key regulator of TG metabolism; individuals carrying loss‐of‐function mutations in this gene exhibit lower levels of circulating TG and remnant cholesterol, along with decreased susceptibility to both type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and ASCVD. A clinical investigation of MAR001, a mAb designed to inhibit ANGPTL4, was conducted through two separate early‐phase trials: a first‐in‐human, placebo‐controlled, single‐ascending‐dose Phase 1 study involving healthy volunteers and participants with hypertriglyceridemia, followed by a randomized, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled Phase 1b/2a trial that included 55 individuals with hypertriglyceridemia and metabolic dysfunction. These studies revealed that MAR001 administration was safe and generally well tolerated, with no observed treatment‐emergent systemic inflammation or alterations in mesenteric lymph node morphology as assessed by MRI; moreover, the 450 mg dose produced placebo‐adjusted mean reductions of 52.7% in TG levels and 52.5% in remnant cholesterol levels at Week 12 [ 158 ]. These results suggest that ANGPTL4 inhibition may attenuate atherosclerotic processes and thereby reduce the incidence of ASCVD events.

3.1.2.1.8 Targeting the Scavenger Receptor for ox‐LDL Studies have shown that lectin‐like oxidized LDL receptor‐1 (LOX‐1) can promote AS and inflammation. A randomized, double‐blind, dose‐finding study showed that a LOX‐1 antagonist (MEDI6570) can significantly reduce soluble LOX‐1 and IL‐6 levels but did not reduce noncalcified coronary plaque volume in patients with residual inflammation after acute MI [ 159 ].

3.1.2.1.9 Bempedoic Acid Bempedoic acid is an inhibitor of ATP citrate lyase (ACLY), an enzyme that plays a key role in lipid synthesis. The CLEAR Outcomes trial demonstrated that bempedoic acid can safely and effectively reduce MACEs in 13,970 statin‐intolerant patients [ 160 ], as well as in high‐risk primary prevention patients [ 161 ].

3.1.2.1.10 Antisense Oligonucleotides (ASOs) Targeting Apolipoprotein (Apo) C‐III Volanesorsen and olezarsen are two ASOs targeting ApoC‐III. Volanesorsen resulted in a 73.9% reduction in TG levels after 3 months of treatment [ 162 ] and the maintenance of 50% lower levels compared with those of the control over 15 months [ 163 ] and significantly reduced hepatic steatosis in patients with familial partial lipodystrophy [ 164 ]. Like volanesorsen, olezarsen, an N‐acetylgalactosamine‐conjugated antisense oligonucleotide, has also been shown to significantly reduce TG levels by 50% at 6 months in patients with high cardiovascular risk [ 165 ] and by more than 50% at 6 months in patients with moderate hypertriglyceridemia [ 166 ]. Whether this magnitude of triglyceride lowering translates into atherosclerotic benefit, however, remained unresolved. Recently, the ESSENCE‐TIMI 73b trial evaluated olezarsen in patients with hypertriglyceridemia at high cardiovascular risk. Despite reducing triglycerides by ∼64% and remnant cholesterol by ∼72%, olezarsen did not reduce noncalcified coronary plaque volume over 12 months compared with placebo (placebo‐adjusted least‐squares mean difference, 2.98% [95% CI, −3.4 to 9.3]; p = 0.36) [ 167 ].

3.1.2.2 Antidiabetic Therapies 3.1.2.2.1 Biguanides Metformin is a foundational drug for the treatment of T2DM, and its clinical value has long surpassed the scope of glycemic control. Its antiatherosclerotic effects are primarily achieved through the activation of AMPK [ 168 ]. As an intracellular energy sensor, AMPK is activated under metabolic stress, subsequently regulating a series of downstream signaling pathways to maintain vascular health [ 169 ]. Metformin protects against AS through a multitarget approach. It improves endothelial function by increasing NO production, which helps blood vessels relax and heal [ 170 , 171 ]. Additionally, it reduces inflammation by blocking key inflammatory pathways and preventing immune cells from building up inside vessel walls, effectively preventing early plaque formation [ 170 , 172 ]. Finally, metformin decreases oxidative stress by decreasing the levels of harmful ROS and promoting the clearance of damaged cell parts (autophagy), ultimately keeping blood vessel cells healthy under stress [ 168 , 171 ]. With respect to clinical evidence, the UKPDS study was the first study to confirm that metformin reduces the risk of macrovascular complications. In the metformin group (maximum dosage of 2550 mg/day), the risk of macrovascular disease was 30% lower than that in the conventional treatment group. The risk of MI was reduced by an even greater 39%. During the subsequent 10‐year posttrial follow‐up, this reduction in the risk of MI and macrovascular endpoints continued [ 173 , 174 ].

3.1.2.2.2 Sodium‐Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors (SGLT2is) These inhibitors were initially designed as purely glucose‐lowering medications that promote urinary glucose excretion by inhibiting the reabsorption of glucose and sodium in the proximal convoluted tubule of the kidney. However, clinical trials have found that their efficacy in slowing AS progression exceeds what would be expected from their diuretic and hypoglycemic effects alone [ 175 ]. Studies utilizing optical coherence tomography (OCT) and coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) have directly demonstrated the remodeling of plaque morphology. For patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), long‐term administration of SGLT2is promoted the transition of coronary plaques toward a stable phenotype. This was characterized by a significant increase in fibrous cap thickness (48 ± 15 µm vs. 26 ± 24 µm in nonusers, p = 0.005) and a reduced lipid arc [ 176 ]. Furthermore, longitudinal CCTA follow‐up cohorts indicated that SGLT2i therapy significantly reversed both the total coronary plaque volume and the percent atheroma volume (PAV) [ 177 ].

3.1.2.2.3 Pioglitazone Belonging to the thiazolidinedione (TZD) class of medications, pioglitazone functions as a synthetic ligand for peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor‐gamma (PPAR‐γ). PPAR‐γ is a nuclear hormone receptor that critically regulates carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, as well as inflammatory responses in vascular tissues [ 178 ]. Beyond its role as a classic insulin sensitizer, pioglitazone effectively counteracts ox‐LDL‐driven intracellular lipid retention by upregulating the expression of the cholesterol efflux transporters ABCA1 and ABCG1 in macrophages. By doing so, it locally inhibits the formation of atherosclerotic plaques within the vascular wall [ 179 ]. The PERISCOPE trial enrolled 543 patients with T2DM and angiographically confirmed CAD who were randomly assigned to receive either pioglitazone or sulfonylurea glimepiride for 18 months [ 180 ]. Intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) findings showed contrasting changes in atherosclerotic burden between the two groups. The change in PAV, which served as the primary efficacy endpoint, significantly increased by 0.73% in the glimepiride group but slightly decreased by 0.16% in the pioglitazone group [ 180 ].

3.1.2.2.4 Glucagon‐Like Peptide‐1 Receptor Agonists (GLP‐1RAs) These drugs were initially developed as glucose‐lowering agents that stimulate insulin secretion while suppressing glucagon release. However, large‐scale cardiovascular outcome trials (CVOTs) have suggested that their efficacy in reducing atherothrombotic events may not be attributable solely to their glycemic effects. The landmark SELECT trial enrolled 17,604 patients with established ASCVD who had overweight/obese but not diabetes, and demonstrated that, compared with placebo, administration of once‐weekly semaglutide (2.4 mg) reduced MACEs risk by 20% over a median follow‐up of 3.3 years (HR: 0.80; 95% CI, 0.72–0.90) [ 181 ]. Moreover, the SUSTAIN‐6 trial found that compared with placebo, once‐weekly semaglutide (0.5 mg and 1.0 mg) significantly reduced MACEs in T2DM patients at high cardiovascular risk (HR: 0.74; 95% CI, 0.58–0.95) [ 182 ]. The LEADER trial further corroborated these findings, revealing that liraglutide reduced MACEs by 13% (HR: 0.87; 95% CI, 0.78–0.97) in 9340 T2DM patients at high cardiovascular risk [ 183 ]. Current guidelines, including the 2023 ESC guidelines and the 2026 American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care, recommend GLP‐1RAs with proven cardiovascular benefit for patients with T2DM and established ASCVD as part of comprehensive cardiovascular risk reduction [ 184 , 185 ]. Imaging studies have directly revealed the plaque‐modifying effects of GLP‐1RAs, with serial CCTA showing significant regression of nonculprit lesion plaque burden and PAV (PAV: −6.1% vs. −0.7%, p = 0.039) in GLP‐1RA‐treated diabetic patients with recent acute coronary syndrome (ACS) [ 186 ], indicating that cardiovascular protection is through direct antiatherosclerotic, anti‐inflammatory, and endothelial effects.

3.1.2.2.5 Dipeptidyl Peptidase‐4 Inhibitors (DPP‐4is) DPP‐4is prolong endogenous incretin signaling by preventing the degradation of glucagon‐like peptide‐1 and glucose‐dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, thereby increasing glucose‐dependent insulin secretion and suppressing glucagon release with a low risk of hypoglycemia and a largely weight‐neutral profile. Experimental and translational studies suggest that DPP‐4 inhibition may attenuate AS by reducing monocyte recruitment, vascular inflammation, oxidative stress, and ED [ 187 ]. However, these potentially favorable vascular effects have not translated into consistent reductions in clinical atherothrombotic events. In major CVOTs, DPP‐4is were generally noninferior for MACEs, but saxagliptin was associated with an increased risk of hospitalization for heart failure [ 188 , 189 , 190 , 191 , 192 ]. Therefore, DPP‐4is should be viewed mainly as glucose‐lowering agents with cardiovascular safety rather than as an established antiatherosclerotic therapy [ 184 ].

3.1.2.3 Antihypertensive Therapies 3.1.2.3.1 Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs) Third‐generation dihydropyridines such as amlodipine and lacidipine selectively inhibit the inward flux of calcium ions across the membranes of VSMCs and cardiomyocytes, thereby reducing peripheral vascular resistance and inducing potent vasodilation. However, their unique anti‐AS advantages are largely derived from their distinctive physicochemical properties. Their high lipophilicity enables them to integrate deeply into the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane, where they exert powerful membrane antioxidant effects. This effectively protects endothelial cells from oxidative stress‐induced damage and lipid peroxidation [ 193 ]. In the CAMELOT trial initiated in 1999, 1997 patients with angiographically documented CAD and normal blood pressure were randomized to receive amlodipine, enalapril, or placebo. Amlodipine reduced the incidence of adverse cardiovascular events compared with placebo (16.6% vs. 23.1%, p = 0.003). In the IVUS substudy of 274 patients, PAV increased in the placebo group (1.3 ± 4.4%, p = 0.001 vs. baseline), whereas the change with amlodipine was not significant ( p = 0.31 vs. baseline). Among patients whose baseline systolic blood pressure exceeded the mean, PAV progression was slower with amlodipine than with placebo (0.2 ± 3.9% vs. 2.3 ± 4.7%, p = 0.02), with no effect below the mean [ 194 ]. The PREVENT study showed that while amlodipine did not alter the angiographic progression of early coronary luminal diameter narrowing, high‐resolution B‐mode ultrasonography revealed a remodeling effect within the carotid artery system. In the placebo group, the carotid intima‐media thickness (CIMT) increased by 0.033 mm; conversely, the amlodipine group exhibited a regression of 0.0126 mm ( p = 0.007). These findings indicate a substantial reversal in the progression of carotid AS [ 195 ].

3.1.2.3.2 ACE Inhibitors The role of ACE inhibitors in the management of atherosclerotic vascular disease was established by the landmark HOPE study. This trial randomized 9297 high‐risk patients—excluding those with heart failure or severe left ventricular dysfunction—to receive either 10 mg of ramipril daily or a placebo [ 196 ]. The SECURE trial, a substudy of the HOPE study, further evaluated 732 patients using highly reproducible B‐mode ultrasonography to measure 12 carotid artery segments. The results found a clear dose‐dependent inhibition of the progression slope in maximum CIMT. The annual progression rate was 0.0217 mm in the placebo group, which decreased to 0.0180 mm in the 2.5 mg ramipril group and reached a nadir of 0.0137 mm in the 10 mg ramipril group (overall intervention effect p = 0.033) [ 197 ].

3.1.3 Revascularization Strategies When pharmacological treatment is ineffective or vascular stenosis is severe, percutaneous interventions and surgical revascularization become important treatment options.

3.1.3.1 Percutaneous Interventions 3.1.3.1.1 Interventional Therapy for Coronary Artery Stenosis This procedure restores blood flow by placing stents or balloons to dilate narrowed coronary arteries. Drug‐eluting stents are a commonly used treatment method, but there is still room for improvement in their coating biocompatibility and drug‐loading capacity. Self‐assembly coating technology offers a thinner, stronger bonding, and more biocompatible alternative for stents [ 198 ]. Recent studies on novel bioresorbable scaffolds, including an iron‐based scaffold (IRONMAN II) [ 199 ] and a poly‐L‐lactic acid‐based scaffold (FUTURE‐III) [ 200 ], have shown noninferiority to contemporary drug‐eluting stents in key efficacy endpoints, with a very low incidence of scaffold thrombosis and promising long‐term outcomes.

3.1.3.1.2 Peripheral Endovascular Intervention This procedure restores blood flow through percutaneous transluminal angioplasty and/or stent placement across various arterial territories. In the carotid artery, the current evidence base for carotid artery stenting (CAS) demonstrates significant context‐dependent heterogeneity. In asymptomatic patients, a meta‐analysis of three modern RCTs (including CREST‐2, SPACE‐2, and ECST‐2) found no significant benefit of CAS over contemporary medical management alone (RR: 0.72; 95% CI, 0.23–2.27) [ 201 ]. In symptomatic carotid stenosis, network meta‐analyses have demonstrated that compared with carotid endarterectomy (CEA), CAS is associated with lower risks of cranial nerve injury, hematoma, and infection [ 202 ]. Current ESC guidelines recommend CEA for selected patients with ≥ 60%–99% asymptomatic carotid stenosis who are at increased risk of stroke, and CEA is preferred over CAS in patients > 70 years old with symptomatic ≥ 50%–99% carotid stenosis [ 203 ]. In lower extremity arterial disease, a network meta‐analysis of 82 RCTs ( n = 12,796) concluded that endovascular device selection should be tailored to the clinical–anatomical context, with drug‐eluting technologies demonstrating superiority for infrapopliteal chronic limb ischemia [ 204 ]. Moreover, the SIRONA trial revealed that compared with paclitaxel‐coated balloons, sirolimus‐coated balloons resulted in noninferior clinical outcomes for femoropopliteal disease at 12 months (90.5% vs. 92.7%, p _noninferiority = 0.003) [ 205 ]. These findings suggest that device selection for lower extremity intervention requires careful anatomic and lesion‐specific consideration, and that the long‐term benefits of drug‐eluting technologies remain uncertain.

3.1.3.2 Surgical Treatments 3.1.3.2.1 Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG) Commonly known as “bypass surgery,” this procedure restores blood flow by grafting new vessels from a location proximal to the stenosed or occluded coronary arteries to a location distal to the stenosis, thereby bypassing the blocked segment and achieving complete myocardial revascularization. In accordance with the guidelines, CABG is recommended as the preferred revascularization strategy in patients with left main CAD (especially when surgical risk is low and the anatomy is complex), in patients with multivessel disease and a SYNTAX score > 22 or with diabetes, and in those for whom complete revascularization cannot be achieved equivalently by PCI [ 206 , 207 ].

3.1.3.2.2 Carotid Endarterectomy This surgical procedure removes atherosclerotic plaques from the inner wall of the carotid artery to restore blood flow and prevent subsequent ischemic stroke. Current guidelines continue to recommend CEA as the standard revascularization strategy for symptomatic carotid stenosis ≥ 50%–99%. For asymptomatic stenosis (≥ 60%–99%), CEA is recommended in select patients with a perioperative stroke/death risk < 3% [ 203 , 208 ].

3.2 Novel Therapeutic Interventions 3.2.1 Gene Therapy 3.2.1.1 ASOs ASOs are considered among the most advanced RNA‐based therapeutic methods. An ASO is composed of single‐stranded DNA, usually containing 13–20 nucleotides, and its effect is to bind to target mRNA to form a double‐stranded complex that is cleaved by RNase H1, thereby inhibiting protein synthesis and downregulating the expression of specific molecular targets [ 209 , 210 ].

3.2.1.1.1 ASOs Targeting ANGPTL3 Vupanorsen, a hepatically targeted antisense oligonucleotide that inhibits ANGPTL3 synthesis, was evaluated in a Phase 2b randomized, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled trial involving 286 adults with a non‐HDL‐C concentration ≥ 100 mg/dL and a TG concentration of 150–500 mg/dL on statin therapy. The trial demonstrated significant dose‐dependent reductions in non‐HDL‐C (up to 27.7%) and TG (up to 56.8%) levels at 24 weeks, although the effects on LDL‐C levels were more modest (up to 16.0%). However, the development program for this drug was discontinued because of safety concerns, specifically the dose‐dependent increases in the hepatic fat fraction and liver enzyme elevation, in addition to a higher incidence of injection‐site reactions [ 211 ].

3.2.1.1.2 ASOs Targeting Lipoprotein (a) [Lp(a)] Pelacarsen is a second‐generation ASO. It targets apo(a) production via chemical modifications that increase stability, reduce toxicity, and enable specific liver uptake. Clinical trials suggested that pelacarsen reduced Lp(a) levels in a dose‐dependent manner by up to 80% in patients with CVD, with a specific study showing Lp(a)‐C reductions of 29%–67% and a neutral to mild effect (2%–19% reduction) on corrected LDL‐C (LDL‐Ccorr) [ 212 ]. 3.2.1.2 siRNAs siRNA can be used for potent and specific gene silencing mediated by double‐stranded RNA, which has successfully transitioned from basic research to clinical research [ 213 , 214 ].

3.2.1.2.1 siRNAs Targeting ANGPTL3 Two siRNAs targeting ANGPTL3 have been reported. Solbinsiran was evaluated in a Phase 2, double‐blind, randomized, placebo‐controlled trial involving 205 adults with mixed dyslipidemia on statin therapy, which demonstrated that compared with placebo, the 400 mg dose (administered subcutaneously on Days 0 and 90) significantly reduced apoB by 14.3% and LDL‐C by 16.8% from baseline on Day 180, with generally well‐tolerated safety profiles [ 215 ]. Similarly, zodasiran, another siRNA of ANGPTL3, has been investigated in two Phase 2 trials: the double‐blind, placebo‐controlled ARCHES‐2 trial ( NCT04832971 ) in 204 adults with mixed hyperlipidemia showed significant dose‐dependent reductions in TG (up to 63% with 200 mg) and LDL‐C (up to 20%) levels [ 216 ], and the open‐label GATEWAY trial ( NCT05217667 ) in 18 patients with HoFH demonstrated that quarterly zodasiran (200 mg or 300 mg) reduced fasting LDL‐C levels by approximately 36%–40% at Month 6, with greater reductions (up to 56%) in those receiving concomitant PCSK9 inhibitor therapy and a favorable safety profile with sustained efficacy during open‐label extension [ 217 ].

3.2.1.2.2 siRNAs Targeting Lp(a) Olpasiran (AMG 890), zerlasiran (SLN360), and lepodisiran (LY3819469) are all investigational GalNAc‐conjugated siRNAs that share the core mechanism of selectively degrading hepatocyte LPA mRNA to inhibit the synthesis of apolipoprotein(a), thereby potently and sustainably lowering circulating Lp(a) levels. Olpasiran, administered subcutaneously every 12 or 24 weeks in 281 participants with established ASCVD, achieved up to a > 95% median reduction in Lp(a) levels in the Phase 2 OCEAN(a)‐DOSE trial [ 218 ]. In a Phase 2 trial, zerlasiran demonstrated a well‐tolerated profile with primarily mild injection‐site reactions and achieved a placebo‐adjusted, time‐averaged reduction in Lp(a) of greater than 80% over 36 weeks across all dosing regimens [ 219 ]. In a Phase 1 trial, lepodisiran demonstrated a well‐tolerated profile with primarily mild injection‐site reactions and achieved dose‐dependent, long‐duration reductions in Lp(a) concentrations, with maximal median reductions ranging from 41% at the 4 mg dose to 97% at the 608 mg dose and a sustained 94% reduction on Day 337 following the 608 mg single dose [ 220 ]. Clinical studies focusing on the effect of Lp(a) reduction on plaque progression and in individuals with ASCVD are currently underway, and we look forward to the results being published (see the “Ongoing clinical trials” section).

3.2.2 Immunotherapy Inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF‐α), IL‐1β, and IL‐6 can induce apoptosis, pyroptosis, and necrosis within plaques, thereby affecting plaque stability and promoting plaque rupture or ulceration. Because AS is driven not only by lipid accumulation but also by chronic vascular inflammation, immunomodulatory strategies have attracted increasing attention as therapeutic approaches distinct from conventional lipid‐lowering therapy.

3.2.2.1 Targeting Inflammatory Factors mAbs targeting IL‐1β and IL‐6 can suppress inflammatory responses and reduce residual inflammatory risk in selected cardiovascular populations. Ziltivekimab, a humanized mAb targeting the ligand IL‐6, reduced the levels of high‐sensitivity C‐reactive protein (hsCRP) and other inflammatory and thrombotic biomarkers in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and high atherosclerotic risk in the RESCUE Phase 2 trial [ 221 ]. Canakinumab, an anti‐IL‐1β mAb, reduced recurrent cardiovascular events in patients after MI with elevated hsCRP levels in the CANTOS trial without altering lipid levels [ 10 ]; however, the trial also demonstrated an increased risk of fatal infections. More recently, low‐dose IL‐2 therapy increased regulatory T‐cell levels and reduced arterial inflammation in ACS patients with residual systemic inflammation in the IVORY Phase 2 trial [ 222 ]. These findings support inflammation as a tractable therapeutic target in atherosclerotic CVD, although patient selection, infection risk, cost, and long‐term safety remain important considerations.

3.2.2.2 Potential Cardiovascular Risks of Immune Checkpoint Modulation Immune checkpoint modulation may have important vascular consequences in patients with AS. Although immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) targeting PD‐1/PD‐L1 or CTLA‐4 are widely used in cancer treatment, clinical and mechanistic evidence indicates that they may disturb vascular immune homeostasis and accelerate atherosclerotic disease. In a matched cohort with an imaging substudy, ICI exposure was associated with a higher incidence of AS‐related cardiovascular events and a faster increase in plaque volume [ 223 ]. A recent retrospective cohort further reported ICI‐associated ASCVD events, including MI, ischemic stroke, coronary revascularization, and acute limb ischemia [ 224 ]. These clinical observations are supported by pathological and single‐cell studies showing that checkpoint pathways are active within human coronary, carotid, and aortic plaques. ICI exposure has been linked to altered plaque inflammatory composition, while recent immune‐checkpoint mapping revealed PD‐1, CTLA4, LAG3, and related checkpoint interactions across plaque immune‐cell networks [ 225 , 226 ]. Recent studies further suggest that plaque‐associated PD‐1+ T‐cell subsets may be key cellular targets of checkpoint modulation, although their effects may depend on the antibody format, immune‐cell state, and plaque context [ 227 , 228 ]. Several registered studies are now evaluating ICI‐associated plaque progression or adverse cardiovascular events, including NCT06519292 and NCT06785974 [ 229 , 230 ]. Thus, checkpoint modulation should not be presented as a uniformly beneficial immune strategy in ASCVD; rather, it highlights the need for cardiovascular risk stratification and monitoring when immune‐activating therapies are used in patients with preexisting atherosclerotic risk.

3.2.2.3 Chemokine‐Targeted Immunotherapy Chemokine pathways are attractive targets for AS because they regulate leukocyte recruitment, macrophage localization, endothelial activation, T‐cell polarization, and plaque inflammation. Key axes include CCL2–CCR2, CXCL12–CXCR4, and CCL5‐related chemokine heterodimers. Clinical translation, however, remains limited. In a randomized, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled Phase 2 study, the CCR2‐blocking mAb MLN1202 reduced circulating hsCRP levels in individuals with atherosclerotic risk factors and elevated baseline CRP levels, supporting the proof‐of‐mechanism for the role of CCR2 blockade in residual inflammatory risk [ 231 ]. This trial did not assess plaque regression or cardiovascular outcomes. A subsequent Phase 2a FDG‐PET/CT study of MLN1202 in patients with stable ASCVD was registered but withdrawn without enrollment, whereas a Phase 1 study is evaluating CCR2‐targeted PET detection in human carotid AS [ 232 , 233 ].

The major challenge is that chemokine signaling is highly context dependent. Broad blockade may be harmful when a chemokine pathway also maintains protective vascular immune niches. For example, mural cell‐derived CCL2 and MIF preserve a homeostatic macrophage niche in viable plaque regions, whereas disruption of this unit aggravates plaque necrosis and inflammation [ 234 ]. Similarly, vascular cell‐specific enhancement of CXCR4 signaling may be atheroprotective, while endothelial‐derived CXCL12 has been linked to AS progression [ 235 , 236 ]. Recent work has also identified a noncanonical chemokine axis in which DC‐derived CCL17 signals through CCR8 on T cells to induce CCL3, thereby suppressing atheroprotective Foxp3 + Tregs and promoting AS [ 237 ]. More selective strategies, such as disrupting pathogenic chemokine heterodimers or timing CCL2–CCR2 inhibition according to circadian leukocyte recruitment, may therefore be preferable to nonspecific systemic inhibition [ 238 , 239 ]. Future chemokine‐targeted therapies will likely require cell‐specific, temporally controlled, or interaction‐selective designs.

3.2.3 Gene‐Editing Therapy 3.2.3.1 Targeting the Low‐Density Lipoprotein Receptor (LDLR) Gene One open‐label, single‐center, nonrandomized trial evaluated the safety and efficacy of NGGT006, an adeno‐associated virus (AAV) vector carrying an optimized human LDLR gene, in patients with HoFH due to LDLR mutations. Three patients received a single injection of NGGT006 at increasing doses (7.5 × 10 1

2 , 1.5 × 10 13 , or 3.0 × 10 13 vg/kg) and were followed for 52 weeks. NGGT006 was generally well tolerated, with no vector‐related severe adverse events; however, transient liver enzyme elevations occurred in all three patients and resolved after sirolimus and methylprednisolone therapy. The patient who received the highest dose achieved a rapid and sustained reduction in LDL‐C levels (from 11.17 to 0.28 mmol/L), which corresponds to an approximately 97.5% decrease. However, the two lower doses did not lead to meaningful LDL‐C reduction, and the long‐term safety and efficacy require further confirmation [ 240 ].

3.2.3.2 Targeting the ANGPTL3 Gene A Phase 1 ascending‐dose trial evaluated CTX310, a lipid nanoparticle (LNP)‐formulated CRISPR‐Cas9 therapy designed to induce loss‐of‐function mutations in the hepatic ANGPTL3 gene, in 15 adults with uncontrolled hypercholesterolemia, hypertriglyceridemia, or mixed dyslipidemia despite maximally tolerated lipid‐lowering therapy. All 15 participants had at least 60 days of follow‐up. The investigational treatment was generally well tolerated, with no dose‐limiting toxicity, and serious adverse events were reported in two participants (13%): one participant had a spinal disk herniation, and the other died suddenly 179 days after receiving the 0.1‐mg/kg dose. Infusion‐related reactions were reported in three participants (20%), and one participant with elevated aminotransferase levels at baseline had a transient elevation in aminotransferase levels. Dose‐dependent reductions in ANGPTL3 levels were observed, with mean decreases of 79.7% and 73.2% at the two highest doses (0.7 and 0.8 mg/kg), indicating successful hepatic gene editing [ 241 ]. These early findings require confirmation in larger populations and with longer term clinical follow‐up.

3.2.3.3 Targeting the PCSK9 Gene VERVE‐101, a first‐in‐class in vivo base editing therapy targeting PCSK9, provided a proof‐of‐concept for durable LDL‐C reduction in the Phase 1b Heart‐1 trial. However, its development was discontinued because of safety concerns (transient liver enzyme increases and platelet decreases) linked to its first‐generation LNP delivery system [ 242 ]. In the subsequent Phase 1b Heart‐2 study of VERVE‐102, a total of 35 patients with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH) or patients with premature CAD were included, with at least 28 days of follow‐up. The results showed that a dose of 1.0 mg/kg could reduce PCSK9 levels by 88% and LDL‐C levels by 62%. This reduction persisted for at least 1 year of follow‐up in 15 patients, and mild‐to‐moderate infusion‐related reactions and transient alanine aminotransferase elevations occurred; aspiration pneumonitis occurred in one participant with gastroesophageal reflux disease [ 243 ]. In addition, another drug, YOLT‐101, is an experimental in vivo gene therapy that leverages adenine base editing and GalNAc‐modified LNP delivery to silence PCSK9. Data from a trial in six adults with HeFH and persistently high LDL‐C levels showed that a single intravenous dose was generally well tolerated; the most common side effects were transient infusion reactions and self‐limited liver enzyme increases. In the highest dose group (0.6 mg/kg, n = 3), dose‐dependent and durable reductions in plasma PCSK9 and LDL‐C levels were observed at 24 weeks, reaching 74.4% and 52.3%, respectively [ 244 ]. These are encouraging outcomes for further clinical development.

3.2.4 Cell Therapy 3.2.4.1 Mesenchymal Stem Cells (MSCs) MSCs are multipotent stromal cells with self‐renewal, multilineage differentiation, immunomodulatory, and tissue‐repair capacities. Experimental and translational studies suggest that MSCs may modulate inflammatory signaling, promote vascular repair, and reduce plaque formation, but clinical evidence for direct antiatherosclerotic efficacy remains limited [ 245 ]. Therefore, MSC‐based approaches should currently be viewed as investigational strategies rather than established therapies for atherosclerotic vascular disease.

3.2.4.2 CAR‐Treg Cell Therapy Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are key suppressors of vascular inflammation, and engineered CAR‐Treg therapy has recently emerged as a cell‐based immunomodulatory strategy for treating AS. Antioxidized LDL‐specific CAR‐Tregs reduced macrophage foam‐cell formation in vitro and attenuated plaque development in AS‐prone mice through cell contact‐mediated suppression and secretion of inhibitory cytokines, suggesting that antigen‐directed Treg therapy may provide local immune suppression within atherosclerotic lesions [ 246 ]. However, this strategy remains at an early preclinical stage, and no human efficacy data exist for CAR‐Treg therapy in atherosclerotic patients. Major translational challenges include maintaining Treg stability and function in the inflammatory plaque microenvironment, ensuring specific homing to lesion sites without systemic immunosuppression, scaling up GMP‐grade manufacturing from low‐abundance Tregs, and establishing long‐term safety and persistence [ 247 , 248 ]. Future studies will need to address these barriers in well‐designed preclinical models prior to any potential clinical testing.

3.2.4.3 Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells (iPSCs) iPSCs are generated by reprogramming somatic cells and can be differentiated into multiple cardiovascular and vascular lineages, including endothelial cells, VSMCs, macrophage‐like cells, and cardiomyocytes. Compared with their more direct application in myocardial repair after infarction, their therapeutic role in AS remains less established. No clinical trial has yet demonstrated iPSC‐based cell therapy as a direct treatment for atherosclerotic vascular lesions. Current registered cardiovascular iPSC studies focus mainly on disease modeling, biobanking, or myocardial regeneration rather than plaque‐targeted therapy. For example, the CAUSE trial used patient‐specific iPSC‐derived endothelial cells to study extreme‐trait CAD and fibromuscular dysplasia, whereas an ongoing iPSC biobank study aims to establish ethnically diverse CVD models [ 249 , 250 ]. In contrast, registered iPSC‐derived cardiomyocyte trials in ischemic cardiomyopathy and heart failure address myocardial regeneration rather than atherosclerotic plaque therapy [ 251 , 252 ].

Nevertheless, iPSC‐derived vascular cells provide useful human platforms for studying AS‐related mechanisms. Haplotype‐edited iPSC‐derived VSMCs have shown that the 9p21.3 CAD risk locus promotes atherogenic‐like VSMC phenotypes, including altered adhesion, contraction, proliferation, and vascular stability [ 253 ]. Another iPSC‐derived VSMC model revealed that the 9p21 risk locus increases vascular calcification, a key feature of advanced atherosclerotic lesions [ 254 ]. More recently, iPSC‐derived endothelial cells exposed to hyperoxic stress developed an AS‐like transcriptional phenotype, supporting their use for modeling ED [ 255 ]. Advances in the generation of iPSC‐derived mural progenitor cells with smooth muscle and pericyte potential may also support vascular repair modeling and future regenerative strategies, although this remains indirect evidence for AS therapy [ 256 ]. Recent work further indicates that the levels of circular RNAs increase during vascular cell differentiation and that these RNAs may serve as biomarkers for vascular disease, expanding the utility of iPSC‐derived vascular models for mechanism discovery and biomarker development [ 257 ]. Overall, the near‐term value of iPSCs in AS lies in patient‐specific disease modeling, vascular organoid construction, mechanism validation, and drug screening. Direct therapeutic use will require further evidence on cell maturity, lineage purity, tumorigenicity, immune compatibility, delivery route, and long‐term behavior within inflammatory plaque microenvironments.
