4 Challenges and Future Directions At present, the clinical treatment of ASCVD has achieved great success. Statins and PCSK9‐targeted therapies can rapidly lower LDL‐C to target levels, yet the residual risk of cardiovascular events remains substantial. This suggests that AS is not merely a lipid disorder [ 3 ]. With the advancement of technology and the discovery of new mechanisms in immunology, neurology, and microbiology, they mark the shift of AS toward multidimensional exploration and precise treatment. However, this shift still faces complex challenges in clinical implementation and translation.

4.1 Translational Barriers In the field of AS drug research, there is a certain discrepancy between preclinical results and clinical efficacy in human clinical trials. Many therapeutic drugs that have performed well in animal models have not shown clinical benefits after they enter clinical trials, highlighting the limitations of current drug development [ 279 ]. For example, in clinical studies on inflammatory pathways, although the CANTOS trial validated the value of the IL‐1β pathway, other drugs did not achieve consistent results. Although colchicine has good therapeutic effects in patients with chronic stable coronary heart disease, it showed a negative result in the CLEAR trial for acute MI [ 280 ]. On the one hand, genetically modified mouse models remain the cornerstone of preclinical research, but they cannot fully reproduce the lethal phenotype of human diseases, as these mice rarely experience spontaneous plaque rupture or acute thrombotic events [ 279 , 281 ]. On the other hand, atherosclerotic plaques in mice usually present a stable phenotype, with a thick fibrous cap, and lack the “vulnerable” characteristics of human thin fibrous cap AS, including large necrotic cores and intraplaque hemorrhage [ 279 ]. In addition, mice have natural resistance to coronary AS, and most of the lesions occur in the aorta and carotid arteries, making it difficult to simulate the unique hemodynamic environment of human coronary arteries. In recent years, researchers have attempted to induce plaque instability using surgical models or novel genetically engineered mouse strains to address the aforementioned shortcomings. However, these models often have severe complications, limiting their application in long‐term drug screening [ 281 ].

Another challenge in translation is that most preclinical studies in animal models of AS have examined only male animals, and even when both sexes are included, adequately powered comparisons with sex as an independent variable remain rare [ 282 ]. Sex is an important determinant of plaque phenotype and clinical course: overall plaque burden and markers of inflammation are greater in men than in women, and although younger women are relatively protected, by the seventh decade the incidence of MI in women surpasses that of men [ 282 ]. Consistent with these clinical observations, age‐stratified in vivo OCT of culprit lesions in ACS showed that plaque rupture and features of plaque vulnerability increased with age in women but not in men, whereas the overall distribution of plaque rupture versus erosion was similar between sexes [ 283 ].

4.2 Technology‐Driven Solutions In recent years, new technologies, including nanotechnology, microphysiological systems, and artificial intelligence (AI), have been used to address these translational challenges. First, nanotechnology makes it possible to deliver drugs precisely to the lesion and stabilize plaques, while also reducing the systemic side effects typically associated with standard therapies. The newly developed confined cascade enzyme nanoreactors possess multiple enzyme‐like activities and can efficiently scavenge ROS within AS plaques through cascade catalysis, thereby alleviating local oxidative stress [ 284 ]. In addition, the researchers engineered platelet membrane‐modified extracellular vesicles derived from M2 macrophages (P‐M2EVs) using a membrane fusion technique. This system mimics the natural interaction between platelets and macrophages, demonstrating enhanced plaque‐targeting ability and tissue penetration in vivo, without obvious systemic toxicity [ 285 ]. Second, microphysiological systems, or “Atherosclerosis‐on‐a‐Chip,” can help bridge the gap between conventional in vitro experiments and in vivo models. This type of platform simulates the complex three‐dimensional structure and hemodynamic environment of human blood vessels, enabling research conditions that are closer to physiological reality [ 286 ]. Recent studies have described dynamic coculture systems comprising human endothelial cells, SMCs, and monocytes. These systems enable the study of atherogenic processes, including monocyte extravasation and foam‐cell formation, and provide a platform for evaluating biological agents whose effects may not be reproduced in rodent models because of species differences [ 287 , 288 ].

Third, spatial transcriptomics and proteomics redefine our understanding of the structure of atherosclerotic plaques by preserving the spatial background of molecular expression in tissue in situ [ 289 ]. For example, new spatial omics studies have shown that macrophage subtypes are not fixed and unchanging but undergo gradual transdifferentiation within the boundary region between the fibrous cap and necrotic core, resulting in a transition from an inflammatory HMOX1 + phenotype to a lipid‐handling TREM2 + phenotype [ 12 ]. In addition, mass spectrometry imaging technology promotes the integration of multimodal spatial omics, which can simultaneously analyze lipidome, proteome, and metabolome at cellular resolution, thereby elucidating heterogeneous intercellular signal exchange, lesion vulnerability, and sex‐specific disease mechanisms within plaques [ 290 ]. In the future, integrating multiomics data with emerging technologies may help advance precision medicine for AS.

Fourth, AI has become integrated into AS research, extending its utility from image diagnosis to risk prediction, basic research, and beyond. In the field of imaging, deep learning algorithms have achieved automated plaque segmentation, calcification score measurement, and precise detection of high‐risk features in CCTA [ 291 ]. The latest Quantitative Cardiovascular Imaging research group consensus statement in 2026 further suggests that personalized drug therapy should be guided by AI‐analyzed total plaque volume percentile curves and that drug therapy should be initiated for the presence of any plaque, while high‐intensity intervention is needed for those with a total plaque volume at or above the 70th percentile [ 291 ]. For risk prediction, machine learning models integrate multiple types of omics data, improving the predictive performance of traditional models and enhancing risk prediction 15 years before disease occurrence [ 292 ]. In terms of basic research, AI integrates multiple types of omics data to reveal cellular heterogeneity and molecular characteristics within plaques and to identify novel diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets [ 293 ]. In the future, the further integration of AI with natural language processing, wearable devices, and multimodal data will drive AS from group‐based diagnosis and treatment toward a precise management model that covers the entire life cycle and individualization.

4.3 Clinical Implementation In real‐world clinical practice, we need to rethink how to diagnose, stratify, and treat AS. The first issue is that there is still a lack of biomarkers that can reflect specific pathological processes of AS. For example, the NICI has been proven to be an important regulatory link in vascular inflammation, but there are no imaging methods or blood biomarkers in clinical practice for evaluating neural activity or neuroimmune crosstalk around the blood vessels of patients [ 2 ]. The perivascular fat attenuation index derived from CCTA is a noninvasive alternative index [ 294 ]. Recent studies have shown that imaging‐defined carotid plaque characteristics are associated with ischemic stroke and that carotid perivascular adipose tissue attenuation is associated with stroke and transient ischemic attack in patients with symptomatic carotid artery disease [ 295 ]. As for trained immunity, it can currently be studied only through the measurement of monocyte cytokine secretion function or epigenetic profiling analysis in experimental settings, which is still far from clinical practice. To support mechanism‐based diagnosis and treatment, these biomarkers need to be developed and validated for clinical use—for example, through PET tracers that target specific immune cells, liquid biopsies that capture cell state‐specific epigenetic signals, or integrated multiomics panels [ 296 ].

The second issue is the combination of treatment strategies. At present, multiple new intervention methods, such as anti‐inflammatory mAbs, RNA drugs, and cellular immune regulation therapies, have entered the clinical development stage, but there is still a lack of clear guidance on how to use them in conjunction with existing therapies. To solve this problem, it is necessary to design a reasonable combination therapy plan to achieve simultaneous intervention in different pathogenic pathways. A Mendelian randomization analysis revealed that simultaneous inhibition of LDL‐C, Lp(a), and the IL‐6 pathway could reduce the risk of coronary heart disease by about 30%, which was significantly better than that associated with the single‐target intervention [ 297 ]. In addition, in the future, patients can be stratified on the basis of the molecular pathological characteristics of plaques, such as phenotypes dominated by SMC proliferation or phenotypes dominated by an inflammatory response, which can aid in the personalized selection of treatment strategies [ 298 ]. However, achieving the above goals requires clinical studies with prospective trial designs and long‐term follow‐up systems to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of the combination regimen.

The third issue involves regulatory science and health economics. Traditional clinical trials require cardiovascular outcomes as the primary endpoint, which typically requires large sample sizes and long‐term follow‐up, but may have a high threshold for the development of new drugs. If regulatory agencies can accept alternative endpoints strongly associated with clinical events in different populations on the basis of sufficient verification, it can accelerate the drug development process [ 299 ]. AI‐based plaque quantification and radiotranscriptomics are advancing plaque characterization. These tools facilitate the validation of alternative endpoints, streamline experimental design, and accelerate clinical research and development decisions [ 291 , 300 ]. Cost also remains a barrier: biologics, gene therapies, and cell‐based products are expensive, and equitable access will depend on value‐based pricing, risk‐sharing agreements, and streamlined manufacturing. Clinical translation will depend on a deeper understanding of disease biology, validated biomarkers, efficient trial designs, workable regulatory pathways, and delivery models that ensure equitable access.

5 Conclusion AS has shifted from being considered a lipid‐storage disorder to a systemic disease shaped by interactions across the vascular, immune, metabolic, and nervous systems. These insights are now being translated into distinct therapies—anti‐inflammatory mAbs, RNA‐based strategies targeting PCSK9, ANGPTL3, and Lp(a), and early‐phase cell and gene‐editing approaches. Looking ahead, the management of AS is moving toward integrated risk assessment. This shift demands that clinical risk stratification evolve beyond single indicators to a comprehensive integration of lipid, inflammatory, and multiomic markers. Therapeutically, future clinical success will rely not on sequential monotherapy, but on selecting tailored combination regimens for individual patients by integrating polygenic risk scores, single‐cell transcriptomic features, and plaque imaging phenotypes. Although challenges remain, continued advances in emerging technologies and mechanistic insights are steadily driving the shift toward personalized, precision therapy for AS.
